## <mark>Erythema Nodosum</mark>

<mark>Erythema nodosum is characterized by a sudden onset of symmetric, tender, erythematous, warm nodules and raised plaques with bilateral distribution, typically located on the anterior aspect of the lower extremities (Figs.</mark> <mark>68-4 and 68-5).</mark> The lesions are most commonly found on the shins. <mark>Initially, the nodules appear vivid red or purplish, evolving over several days to a yellow or greenish hue, resembling a deep bruise—a feature known as *erythema contusiforme*.</mark> <mark>Ulceration does not occur, and healing takes place without atrophy or scarring.</mark>

Acute episodes of erythema nodosum are often accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, malaise, arthralgia, headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, cough, or diarrhea. The eruption typically lasts 3 to 6 weeks, and recurrences are common.

Clinical variants such as erythema nodosum migrans, subacute nodular migratory panniculitis of Vilanova and Pinol, and chronic erythema nodosum are now considered part of the spectrum of erythema nodosum rather than distinct entities.

### Etiology

<mark>Erythema nodosum is associated with a wide range of underlying conditions, including:</mark>

- <mark>**Infections** (e.g., streptococcal infections—most common in children; also tuberculosis, Yersinia, Mycoplasma, fungal infections)</mark>
- **Medications** (e.g., sulfonamides, oral contraceptives, penicillins)
- **Malignancies** (e.g., lymphoma, leukemia)
- <mark>**Autoimmune and inflammatory diseases** (e.g., sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease—most common in adults)</mark>
- **Pregnancy**
- **Idiopathic** (a significant number of cases have no identifiable cause)

<mark>It is regarded as a hypersensitivity reaction to various inciting agents.</mark>

### <mark>Histopathology</mark>

<mark>Erythema nodosum is the classic example of **mostly septal panniculitis without vasculitis**.</mark> <mark>Key histologic features include:</mark>

- <mark>Thickened connective tissue septa of the subcutis infiltrated with inflammatory cells extending into periseptal fat.</mark>
- <mark>Inflammatory infiltrate composition varies with lesion age:</mark>
  <mark>- **Early lesions**: Predominance of neutrophils.</mark>
  <mark>- **Late lesions**: Histiocytes, small granulomas, and multinucleated giant cells.</mark>
- <mark>**Miescher radial granuloma**: A characteristic finding consisting of small, round aggregates of histiocytes arranged radially around a central slit-like cleft. The nature of this cleft remains unknown, with no evidence of endothelial lining on ultrastructural or immunohistochemical studies.</mark>
- <mark>In older lesions, histiocytes may coalesce into multinucleated giant cells that retain a stellate cleft reminiscent of the Miescher granuloma.</mark>
- <mark>**Absence of vasculitis** is a critical diagnostic feature.</mark>
- <mark>Late-stage changes include granulation tissue at the septal-fat interface and fibrosis, but resolution occurs without scarring or atrophy.</mark>

### Treatment

Management focuses on identifying and treating the underlying condition.

- Most cases resolve spontaneously within a few weeks.
- Supportive measures such as bed rest may be sufficient.
- Symptomatic relief can be achieved with:
  - **Aspirin**
  - **Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)**
  - **Saturated solution of potassium iodide** (2–10 drops daily), which may accelerate resolution
- **Systemic corticosteroids** are rarely necessary and should be avoided unless absolutely indicated, particularly if an underlying infection has not been ruled out.

---

# <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>

<mark>Classically, lesions are divided into two categories: **specific** and **non-specific**.</mark> <mark>Specific cutaneous lesions contain granulomas on histopathologic examination, whereas non-specific skin findings are reactive and do not exhibit sarcoidal granulomas.</mark>

## Specific Lesions

Specific sarcoidal lesions most often appear on the head and neck (Figs. 153-2, 153-3, and 153-4) but may occur symmetrically or asymmetrically on any part of the skin and mucosa. Lesions can present in various morphologies, including macules, papules, patches, plaques, and nodules. Scalp involvement may lead to alopecia, and nail changes can also occur. These lesions may be scaly, telangiectatic, or atrophic. Although diverse in appearance, several clinical presentations are classically associated with cutaneous sarcoidosis.

The most common presentation is the **papular form** (see Figs. 153-2, 153-3, and 153-4). These firm, 2- to 5-mm papules typically have a translucent red-brown or yellow-brown hue. The yellow-brown color is often described as resembling "apple jelly," a feature enhanced with diascopy (Fig. 153-5). Diascopy may also reveal the underlying nodular quality of the granulomas. However, this finding is not pathognomonic for sarcoidosis, as other granulomatous conditions such as lupus vulgaris may show similar characteristics. The lesions often have a waxy appearance due to mild epidermal atrophy, though epidermal changes vary. Papular lesions predominantly affect the face and neck, especially the periorbital skin (see eFig. 153-5.1 in online edition).

Over time, papular lesions may coalesce into **annular plaques** (Fig. 153-6), **non-annular plaques** (Fig. 153-7 and see eFig. 153-7.1 in online edition), or **nodules** (Fig. 153-8), which may retain the translucent quality of the original papules.

**Lupus pernio** refers to symmetric, violaceous, indurated plaques and nodules affecting the nose, earlobes, cheeks, and digits (Figs. 153-9, 153-10, and 153-11). This variant is distinctive and strongly associated with systemic disease, particularly chronic upper respiratory tract involvement. Lesions of lupus pernio may extend into the nasal sinuses and are often progressive and disfiguring.

# Etiology and Pathogenesis

Etiology of capillary malformations (CM) is currently unknown. <mark>Facial CM is thought to result from clonal expansion of abnormal cells originating from the neural crest.</mark> The identification of the affected gene (*RASA1*) in CM-AVM (see Arteriovenous Malformations) may provide insights into the pathogenesis of the more common sporadic CM.

Histologically, CM is characterized by dilatation of a normal number of capillaries in the papillary and upper reticular dermis, along with areas showing an increased number of otherwise normal-appearing capillaries (see Fig. 173-2). Endothelial cells are flat. Factor VIII, fibronectin, and basement membrane proteins are normal, but S100 staining reveals abnormal innervation.

# CAPILLARY MALFORMATIONS AT A GLANCE

- **Worldwide occurrence**: Affects approximately 0.1% to 0.2% of the population  
- **Type**: Congenital no-flow malformations of the capillary bed  
- <mark>**Color**: Pinkish-red to purple; tends to darken and thicken over time</mark>  
- <mark>**Clinical significance**: In most cases, a cosmetic concern</mark>  
- <mark>**Syndromic associations**: Can be part of Sturge-Weber syndrome, Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome, or phakomatosis pigmentovascularis</mark>  
- **Pathology**: Capillaries are increased in size and number, with evidence of abnormal innervation  

# Clinical Findings

## CUTANEOUS LESIONS (Fig. 173-3; See Fig. 173-2)

Capillary malformations (CM) present as red, homogenous, congenital lesions that are typically unilateral, occasionally bilateral, and rarely midline. They involve the skin and subcutis, and sometimes mucosa.  

- **Color**: Ranges from pinkish-red to deep purple  
- **Shape**: Geographic borders or dermatomal distribution  
- **Texture**: Flat, painless, non-blanching (under pressure), do not bleed spontaneously, and are not warm to touch  
- **Distribution**: Can occur anywhere on the body; 50% are located on the face, following the trigeminal nerve branches:
  - **V1 (ophthalmic)**: Forehead, upper eyelid  
  - **V2 (maxillary)**: Lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip  
  - **V3 (mandibular)**: Lower lip, chin, mandible  

CM may be associated with other vascular malformations as part of a syndrome, such as:
- <mark>**Sturge-Weber syndrome**</mark>
- <mark>**Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome**</mark>
- **Servelle-Martorell syndrome**
- **Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis**

These syndromes are not inherited.  

Rarely, CM in the lumbosacral region may be a cutaneous marker of occult spinal dysraphism.

# <mark>ATYPICAL/DYSPLASTIC NEVI</mark>

# <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

- Prevalence among Caucasian young adults roughly 10 percent; varies by population  
- <mark>Flat (totally or partially), large (>5 mm) lesions with irregular shape, indistinct borders, and variable pigmentation</mark>  
- <mark>Risk markers for melanoma and potential precursors of melanoma</mark>  
- <mark>Most frequent on sun-exposed areas, especially intermittently exposed sites such as the back</mark>  
- Associated with large numbers of common acquired nevi  
- Majority of lesions will involute and disappear over time  
- Histologic features include presence of an immature or disordered growth pattern, lymphocytic host response, and random cytologic atypia in melanocytes  

<mark>The usual clinical criteria for the diagnosis of a dysplastic nevus (DN) are two obligate features:</mark>  
1. <mark>Diameter in one dimension at least 5 mm</mark>  
2. <mark>A prominent flat component</mark>  

<mark>Plus two of the following three additional features:</mark>  
- <mark>Irregular, asymmetric outline</mark>  
- <mark>Indistinct borders</mark>  
- <mark>Variable pigmentation</mark>  

Histologically, DNs show an immature or disordered growth pattern, a lymphocytic host response, and random cytologic atypia in melanocytes.

Both clinical and histologic criteria for dysplastic nevi are reproducible across observers.

Most epidemiologic data on DNs come from studies of melanoma etiology. In nearly every study assessing melanoma risk associated with DNs, these nevi are linked to an increased risk of melanoma. Clinical diagnosis of DN has typically been used as the risk factor in these analyses. Approximately 10 percent of adults of northern European descent have DNs, based on multiple case-control studies of melanoma risk. Prevalence in control populations across studies ranges from 7 to 24 percent, with variation attributed to geographic region, control selection methods, and differences in diagnostic criteria. Despite these variations, the findings are remarkably consistent.

Limited data exist on the population prevalence of DNs, and geographic and racial differences are likely. One early cross-sectional study in a general population supports this variability.

# CHAPTER 123  
# Atypical Melanocytic Nevi  

**Margaret A. Tucker**  

## EPIDEMIOLOGY  

The term *atypical melanocytic nevi* includes several clinical entities, such as common atypical dysplastic nevi, rare atypical Spitz or spitzoid nevi, atypical genital nevi, and other unusual melanocytic nevi. This chapter focuses on the common atypical/dysplastic nevi, which are relatively frequent melanocytic neoplasms.  

Atypical nevi were first recognized as distinct pigmented lesions during the clinical assessment of melanoma-prone families. The nomenclature for these lesions includes **B-K moles** (named after the first two families described, whose surnames began with B and K), **familial atypical multiple mole and melanoma syndrome**, **atypical mole syndrome**, **Clark's nevus**, and **nevus with architectural disorder** (with varying degrees of melanocytic atypia). The terminology has been historically contentious. Currently, the term **dysplastic nevus (DN)** is more commonly used for both clinical and histologic diagnoses, and it is the author’s preferred term. Thus, this term will be used throughout the chapter.  

<mark>The usual clinical criteria for diagnosing a DN include two obligate features:</mark>  
- <mark>Diameter of at least **5 mm** in one dimension</mark>  
- <mark>A **prominent flat component**</mark>  

<mark>Plus **two of the following three features**:</mark>  
- <mark>Irregular, asymmetric outline</mark>  
- <mark>Indistinct borders</mark>  
- <mark>Variable pigmentation</mark>  

<mark>*(See Fig.</mark> 123-1)*  

<mark>Histologically, dysplastic nevi show:</mark>  
- <mark>**Disordered or immature growth pattern**</mark>  
- <mark>**Lymphocytic host response**</mark>  
- <mark>**Random cytologic atypia in melanocytes**</mark>  

*(See Fig. 123-2)*  

Multiple studies have demonstrated that the clinical and histologic features of dysplastic nevi are associated with an increased risk of melanoma, particularly in individuals with familial melanoma syndromes.  

## ATYPICAL/DYSPLASTIC NEVI  
### AT A GLANCE  

*(Image placeholder: Clinical and dermoscopic appearance of dysplastic nevi illustrating irregular borders, color variation, and flat morphology)*

## <mark>Nevomelanocytic Neoplasms</mark>

Nevomelanocytic neoplasias are commonly subcategorized based on the location of nevus cells:  
- <mark>**Junctional**: cells located in the epidermis</mark>  
- <mark>**Intradermal**: cells located in the dermis</mark>  
- <mark>**Compound**: cells present in both the epidermis and dermis</mark>  

Pathologically, nevus cells in the deeper dermis tend to be smaller and show reduced expression of melanocytic antigens.

### Clinical Features
- <mark>Lesions are typically uniform in appearance and small in size</mark>  
- <mark>Primarily develop during childhood and young adulthood</mark>  
- Increased numbers of acquired nevi are associated with an elevated risk for melanoma (see Chap. 124)  

### <mark>Synonyms</mark>
Commonly used terms include:  
- Nevus cell nevus  
- Nevocellular nevus  
- Nevocytic nevus  
- Soft nevus  
- Neuronevus  
- Pigmented nevus  
- Pigmented mole  
- Common mole  
- Melanocytic nevus  
- Hairy nevus  
- Cellular nevus  
- Benign melanocytoma  

### Epidemiology

The number of nevi varies with age and sex:  
- **First decade**: median of 0 (males), 2 (females)  
- **Second decade**: 10 (males), 16 (females)  
- **Third decade**: 16 (males), 24 (females)  
- **Fourth decade**: 10 (males), 19 (females)  
- **Fifth decade**: 12 (males), 15 (females)  
- **Sixth decade**: 4 (males), 12 (females)  
- **Seventh to ninth decades**: 2.0 (males), 3.5 (females)  

In a study of Australian whites:  
- Average nevus count peaked at **43 in males** and **27 in females** during the second and third decades, respectively  
- Numbers declined significantly by the sixth and seventh decades  

Similar age-related patterns have been observed globally. Gender differences in nevus prevalence are not consistently evident, though most studies report nearly equal distribution between males and females.

### Ethnic and Phenotypic Variations
- Prevalence of acquired nevi varies by ethnicity  
- In African populations, individuals with lighter skin have a higher nevus count than those with darker skin  
- In prepubertal white children, higher nevus counts are associated with:  
  - Pale skin  
  - Blue or green eyes  
  - Blond or light-brown hair  
  - Tendency to sunburn  
  - *No significant association with freckling*  
- Other studies report variable associations with these phenotypic traits

### Environmental Factors
- **Ultraviolet radiation (UVR)** is a key contributing factor in nevus development  
- In Australia, nevus density increases with higher ambient sun intensity in northern regions  
- Use of UVR-blocking sunscreens in children has been shown to reduce the formation of new nevi

### Genetic Influences
- Family aggregation of nevus size, number, and distribution is well documented  
- Strong hereditary component, particularly evident in **atypical nevi** and **familial melanoma** syndromes  
- Also relevant in **congenital melanocytic nevi (CNN)**

### Immune-Mediated Phenomena
- Acquired nevi can be targeted by the immune system, leading to **halo nevus** formation  
- In a study of 8,298 white adolescents (12–16 years):  
  - **1.2% of males** (51 individuals)  
  - **0.5% of females** (22 individuals)  
  - Overall prevalence: **0.9%**  
- In a large series of halo nevi:  
  - Age range: 3 to 42 years  
  - Mean age: 15 years  
  - Most cases occur before age 20

## Etiology and Pathogenesis

The exact origin of nevi remains unclear, despite numerous theories and some supporting evidence.

### Current Understanding:
- Nevomelanocytic nevi are **clonal proliferations**  
- A **B-RAF V600E mutation** is identified in the majority of:  
  - Common acquired nevi  
  - Atypical (dysplastic) nevi  
  - Congenital nevi  
- This mutation is thought to play a central role in nevus initiation  

### Exceptions:
- **B-RAF mutations are not commonly found** in:  
  - Blue nevi  
  - Spitz nevi  

Thus, while B-RAF activation is a key driver in most melanocytic nevi, alternative molecular pathways likely underlie other nevus subtypes.

## <mark>Treatment of Severe Nodular/Conglobate Acne</mark>

### <mark>High Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin** is strongly recommended as monotherapy for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne due to its superior efficacy compared to systemic antibiotics or topical therapy alone.</mark>

### <mark>Medium Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with the fixed-dose combination of **adapalene and benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**, or with **azelaic acid**, can be recommended for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>

### <mark>Low Strength of Recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics** in combination with **adapalene** or **BPO** can be considered for the treatment of severe nodular/conglobate acne.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with systemic antibiotics and topical treatments (excluding topical antibiotics) can be considered.</mark>
- <mark>For females: **Hormonal anti-androgens** in combination with a topical treatment (excluding antibiotics) can also be considered.</mark>

### Open Recommendation
- Due to insufficient evidence, no recommendation can be made for or against the use of **intense pulsed light (IPL)** or **laser therapy** in severe nodular/conglobate acne.
- Although **photodynamic therapy (PDT)** shows effectiveness, it cannot currently be recommended due to lack of standardized treatment protocols and concerns about acute adverse reactions.

### <mark>Negative Recommendation</mark>
- **Topical monotherapy** is not recommended for conglobate acne.
- **Oral antibiotics** are not recommended as monotherapy.
- **Oral anti-androgens** are not recommended as monotherapy.
- **Artificial UV radiation sources** are not recommended.
- **Visible light therapy** as monotherapy is not recommended.

---

## Choice of Topical vs. Systemic Treatment

There is limited evidence directly comparing topical and systemic therapies or evaluating the added benefit of combination therapy over topical treatment alone. Most studies compare topical antibiotic monotherapy with systemic antibiotic monotherapy.

<mark>In clinical practice, expert consensus supports that:</mark>
- <mark>Patients with **severe papulopustular acne** or **moderate nodular acne** achieve better outcomes with **systemic antibiotic plus topical treatment**, or with **systemic isotretinoin**.</mark>
- <mark>Involvement of the trunk is a key factor favoring systemic therapy.</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic treatments** are associated with better adherence and higher patient satisfaction, particularly in widespread disease.</mark>

---

## Additional Considerations

- <mark>**Isotretinoin** is highly effective in severe cases, supported by strong clinical experience despite limited controlled trial data specific to nodular/conglobate forms.</mark>
- Evidence for many treatment options was downgraded due to reliance on indirect data from studies of severe papulopustular acne, particularly when assessing nodule and cyst reduction.
- Prescribers should be mindful of the risk of **antibiotic resistance** when using systemic antibiotics.
- Systemic antibiotics such as **doxycycline** and **lymecycline** should be limited to a maximum treatment duration of **3 months**.
- In cases where higher-strength recommendations cannot be followed (due to cost, availability, licensing, or legal restrictions), lower-strength alternatives may be used as first-line therapy.

---

## Treatment of Papulopustular Acne

There is insufficient evidence to recommend laser or light-based therapies (other than blue light) for papulopustular acne due to lack of standardized protocols, clinical trial data, and real-world experience.

Systemic treatment with **isotretinoin** is recommended in severe cases based on high efficacy observed in clinical practice, although safety and tolerability data remain limited and insufficient for guiding recommendations independently.

# <mark>Negative recommendation</mark>

- **Topical antibiotics as monotherapy** are not recommended for the treatment of mild to moderate papulopustular acne.  
- **Artificial UV radiation** is not recommended for the treatment of mild to moderate papulopustular acne.  
- The **fixed-dose combination of erythromycin and zinc** is not recommended for the treatment of mild to moderate papulopustular acne.  
- <mark>**Systemic therapy with anti-androgens, antibiotics, and/or isotretinoin** is not recommended for the treatment of mild to moderate papulopustular acne.</mark>

> **Note:** Limitations such as financial constraints, reimbursement policies, legal restrictions, drug availability, or licensing may necessitate the use of a lower-strength treatment as first-line therapy.  
> Prescribers should be aware of the risk of antibiotic resistance when prescribing antibiotics.

---

# <mark>Recommendations for severe papulopustular/moderate nodular acne</mark>

## <mark>High strength of recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Oral isotretinoin monotherapy** is strongly recommended.</mark>

## <mark>Medium strength of recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics**<sup>2,3</sup> in combination with:</mark>
  <mark>- **adapalene**<sup>4</sup>,</mark>
  <mark>- the **fixed-dose combination of adapalene and benzoyl peroxide (BPO)**, or</mark>
  <mark>- **azelaic acid**<sup>5</sup></mark>  
  <mark>can be recommended.</mark>

## <mark>Low strength of recommendation</mark>
- <mark>**Systemic antibiotics**<sup>2,3</sup> in combination with **BPO**<sup>5</sup> can be considered.</mark>
- <mark>**For females:** Hormonal anti-androgens in combination with:</mark>
  <mark>- systemic antibiotic<sup>2,3</sup> and topicals (excluding topical antibiotics), or</mark>
  <mark>- a topical treatment (excluding topical antibiotics)</mark>  
  can be considered.

## Open recommendation
- Due to insufficient evidence, no recommendation can be made for or against the use of **red light, IPL, laser, or photodynamic therapy (PDT)** in the treatment of severe papulopustular/moderate nodular acne.
- Although **PDT** is effective, a recommendation cannot be made due to lack of standardized treatment regimens and concerns about acute adverse reactions.

## Negative recommendation
- **Single or combined topical monotherapy** is not recommended.
- **Oral antibiotics as monotherapy** are not recommended.
- **Oral anti-androgens as monotherapy** are not recommended.
- **Visible light as monotherapy** is not recommended.
- **Artificial UV radiation** is not recommended.  

> **Note:** Limitations such as financial resources, reimbursement, legal restrictions, availability, or drug licensing may affect treatment choices.  
> Prescribers should remain vigilant about the risk of antibiotic resistance.

## Clinical Question 1: For which acne forms is systemic isotretinoin indicated?

### Summary of Acne Severity and Isotretinoin Indications

| Acne Type | Clinical Features | Predominant Lesion Type | Severity |
|----------|-------------------|--------------------------|--------|
| Comedonal | Predominantly comedones (open and closed) | Comedonal | Mild to moderate |
| Mild to moderate papulopustular | Papules and pustules, few comedones | Inflammatory or mixed | Mild to moderate |
| Severe papulopustular (may have some nodules) | Widespread papules, pustules, comedones, occasional nodules | Inflammatory/mixed | Severe |
| Very severe (nodular/conglobate) | Extensive inflammation, nodules, cysts, scarring | Nodular/conglobate | Very severe |

**Grading:**
- **4: Severe** – Entire face involved with numerous papules, pustules, comedones, and rare nodules.
- **5: Very Severe** – Highly inflammatory acne with nodules and cysts; may involve face, trunk, or both.

---

### <mark>Indications for Systemic Isotretinoin</mark>

#### <mark>**European Directive (2016 S3 Guidelines)**</mark>
- <mark>**Recommended for:**</mark>
  <mark>- Severe papulopustular acne</mark>
  <mark>- Moderate to severe nodular or conglobate acne</mark>
- <mark>**Strength of Recommendation (SOR):** High</mark>
- <mark>**Positioning:** Second-line therapy after failure of antibiotics and topical treatments</mark>
- <mark>**Important Note:** Oral isotretinoin should only be used in severe, nodular, or conglobate acne that is unresponsive to appropriate topical and systemic therapies.</mark>
- <mark>**Legal Consideration:** Deviating from this guidance may expose prescribers to liability if adverse outcomes occur.</mark>

#### <mark>**Canadian Clinical Practice Guideline (2016)**</mark>
- <mark>**Recommended for:** Severe acne (including cystic/conglobate)</mark>
- <mark>**Strength of Recommendation:** High</mark>
- <mark>**Positioning:** **First-line therapy** in severe, scarring, or refractory acne</mark>
- <mark>**Rationale:** Based on high efficacy, long-term remission rates, safety profile, and patient preference</mark>
- <mark>**Definition of High SOR:** Action strongly recommended; definitely use</mark>

#### <mark>**Expert Consensus and Flexibility**</mark>
- <mark>Despite the European directive, many experts support **first-line use** of isotretinoin in:</mark>
  <mark>- Severe, scarring acne</mark>
  <mark>- Acne with significant psychosocial impact</mark>
  <mark>- Acne unresponsive to conventional therapy (refractory)</mark>
  <mark>- Patients at high risk for scarring</mark>
- <mark>**Limitations** (e.g., cost, access, legal or licensing issues) may require use of lower-SOR treatments even when isotretinoin is clinically preferred.</mark>

---

### Dosing Recommendations

| Parameter | European Guidelines | Canadian Guidelines | Expert Consensus |
|--------|---------------------|---------------------|------------------|
| **Daily Dose** | – | 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day | Start ≤0.5 mg/kg/day; increase to 1 mg/kg/day as tolerated |
| | | | Often: 0.5 mg/kg for first 4 weeks, then 1 mg/kg |
| **Dosing Frequency** | Not specified (once vs. twice daily) | Not specified | Splitting dose may improve tolerance |
| **Cumulative Dose Target** | – | – | 120–150 mg/kg (associated with lower relapse rates) |
| **Duration of Treatment** | 16–24 weeks for nodular/conglobate acne | Until full clearance + 1 month | Individualized; typically 16–20 weeks |

---

### Key Takeaways

- **Isotretinoin is indicated for severe, nodular, conglobate, or scarring acne.**
- **European guidelines** position it as **second-line** after antibiotic failure.
- **Canadian and expert consensus guidelines** support **first-line use** in severe or high-risk cases.
- **Dosing:** Start low (≤0.5 mg/kg), escalate to 0.5–1 mg/kg/day; aim for cumulative dose of 120–150 mg/kg.
- **Treatment duration:** Continue until complete clearance plus ~1 month, or for at least 16–24 weeks.
- **Clinical judgment, patient factors, and access limitations** influence real-world prescribing.

## <mark>Clinical Features of PMLE</mark>

<mark>In any given patient, polymorphic light eruption (PMLE) outbreaks tend to affect the same exposed skin sites consistently, usually in a symmetric pattern.</mark> <mark>The extent of involvement may gradually spread or recede over time.</mark> Not all sun-exposed skin is affected—typically, only certain areas develop lesions, often those that are intermittently exposed or normally covered. Large regions of exposed skin may remain spared.

An extreme example is **juvenile spring eruption**, which primarily affects boys in the spring and presents with pruritic papules and vesicles localized to the ear helices. In some cases, typical PMLE may coexist.

Systemic symptoms are rare in PMLE, but isolated reports include malaise, nausea, and other nonspecific sensations.

## <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>

<mark>PMLE exhibits a wide range of morphologic presentations, all likely sharing similar pathogenesis and prognosis.</mark> <mark>Described forms include:</mark>

- <mark>**Papular** (most common)</mark>
- <mark>**Papulovesicular**</mark>
- <mark>**Plaque**</mark>
- <mark>**Vesiculobullous**</mark>
- <mark>**Insect bite-like**</mark>
- <mark>**Erythema multiforme-like**</mark>

<mark>Pruritus without visible lesions may rarely occur, but a macular variant has not been clearly documented.</mark>

<mark>The **papular form** is characterized by small or large, discrete or confluent lesions that often cluster.</mark> <mark>This is followed in frequency by the papulovesicular and plaque types; other forms are uncommon.</mark>

An **eczematous variant** has been reported, but such cases likely represent mild chronic actinic dermatitis or photo-exacerbated seborrheic or atopic eczema rather than true PMLE.

<mark>Different morphologic variants can occur simultaneously at different body sites in the same individual.</mark> <mark>For example, diffuse facial erythema and swelling may accompany typical papular lesions elsewhere.</mark>

A variant known as **benign summer light eruption**, recognized in continental Europe, refers to small papular PMLE that spares the face and develops after several days of continued sun exposure.

## Laboratory Tests

### Histology

Histopathologic findings in PMLE are characteristic but not pathognomonic and vary with lesion morphology. Common features include:

- Moderate to dense **perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate** in the upper and mid dermis
- Predominance of **T cells**, with occasional neutrophils and rare eosinophils
- **Upper dermal and perivascular edema**
- **Endothelial cell swelling**

Epidermal changes may be absent or include:

- Variable **spongiosis**
- Occasional **dyskeratosis**
- **Exocytosis** of lymphocytes
- **Basal cell vacuolization**

### Blood Tests

Recommended laboratory evaluations include:

- **Antinuclear antibody (ANA)** and **extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibody** testing to exclude subacute cutaneous or other forms of lupus erythematosus
- **Red blood cell protoporphyrin** measurement if erythropoietic protoporphyria is suspected, particularly in cases with diagnostic uncertainty

### Phototesting

- **Monochromator phototesting** confirms photosensitivity in up to 50% of PMLE cases but lacks specificity for distinguishing PMLE from other photodermatoses.
- **Provocation testing** using a solar simulator or broadband light source—sometimes repeated over 2–3 consecutive days—can often reproduce the eruption. This may aid diagnosis and allow biopsy when clinical and historical features are inconclusive.

## Differential Diagnosis

See Box 90-1.

## Complications

While most patients with PMLE do not develop other systemic diseases, a small subset may go on to develop **lupus erythematosus**. Additionally, there is an increased prevalence of prior PMLE among patients diagnosed with lupus, suggesting a possible association between the two conditions.

# <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

## <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>

<mark>Molluscum contagiosum (MC) typically presents as small, pink, pearly, or flesh-colored papules that gradually enlarge, occasionally reaching up to 3 cm in size—referred to as "giant molluscum." As the lesions grow, they often develop a characteristic dome-shaped, opalescent appearance with a central depression or umbilication (Fig.</mark> 195-12A). <mark>A white, curd-like material can be expressed from this central core.</mark>

Most individuals develop multiple papules, commonly located in intertriginous areas such as the axillae, popliteal fossae, and groin. Genital and perianal lesions may occur in children and are rarely indicative of sexual transmission in this age group.

Lesions may appear in clusters or in a linear arrangement, the latter often due to koebnerization—development of new lesions at sites of skin trauma. Perilesional erythema and eczematous changes, known as molluscum dermatitis, can occur. Erythematous lesions (see Fig. 195-12B) are thought to represent an immune response to the virus.

In patients with advanced HIV infection or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, molluscum lesions may be extensive, large, and widespread, affecting both genital and extragenital sites.

# <mark>Special Tests</mark>

<mark>Diagnosis is usually clinical, but confirmation can be obtained when needed by examining the central core material.</mark> <mark>A crush preparation of the lesion contents followed by Giemsa staining may reveal characteristic findings (Fig.</mark> 195-13).

Histopathologic examination shows epidermal hyperplasia and hypertrophy. Above the basal layer, enlarged keratinocytes contain large intracytoplasmic inclusions known as Henderson-Paterson bodies (Fig. 195-14). These inclusions increase in size as infected cells migrate toward the stratum corneum.

# Differential Diagnosis

Consider the following in the differential diagnosis:
- **Verrucae** (common warts)
- **Pyogenic granulomas**
- **Amelanotic melanoma**
- **Basal cell carcinomas**
- **Appendageal tumors**

In immunocompromised patients, fungal infections such as **cryptococcosis**, **histoplasmosis**, and **penicilliosis** should also be considered.

# Complications

While many patients are asymptomatic, complications may include:
- **Pruritus**, particularly problematic in individuals with underlying atopic dermatitis
- **Chronic conjunctivitis** and **punctate keratitis** in cases involving eyelid lesions
- **Secondary bacterial infection**, especially when lesions are scratched or excoriated

## <mark>Acanthosis Nigricans</mark>

<mark>In some cases, oral, esophageal, pharyngeal, laryngeal, conjunctival, and anogenital mucosal surfaces may be involved.</mark> <mark>In general, however, the back of the neck is the most consistently and severely affected area.</mark> <mark>The development of superimposed **acrochordons** in involved areas is well described.</mark> <mark>In particularly florid cases, involvement on the back of the hands over the knuckles and even on the palms can be seen.</mark> <mark>When the palms are involved, the rugated appearance of the palmar surface has been called **tripe palms** and is usually associated with acanthosis nigricans seen in the setting of malignancy.</mark>

<mark>In the majority of cases, the most important factor in diagnosing acanthosis nigricans is recognizing the usually associated **hyperinsulinemia**, which is a known risk factor for type 2 diabetes.</mark>

### Histopathology
<mark>The histopathology of clinical lesions demonstrates **papillomatosis** and **hyperkeratosis** but minimal acanthosis.</mark> <mark>Hyperpigmentation of the basal layer has been variably demonstrated, and the brown color of the lesions is attributed to hyperkeratosis by most.</mark>

### <mark>Treatment</mark>
<mark>Treatment of acanthosis nigricans is generally ineffective.</mark> <mark>Topical treatments with **calcipotriol**, **salicylic acid**, **urea**, and systemic or topical **retinoids** have all been used with anecdotal success.</mark> <mark>When identifiable, treatment of the underlying cause may be beneficial.</mark> <mark>Improvement or resolution does occur with **weight loss** in some obese patients.</mark> <mark>Medications that improve insulin sensitivity, such as **metformin**, have a theoretic benefit.</mark> <mark>Removal of an offending medication generally results in clearance of the skin.</mark>

<mark>In patients with acanthosis nigricans associated with malignancy, there is usually improvement following treatment of the underlying malignancy.</mark> <mark>The skin finding may present before or after the diagnosis of malignancy is made.</mark> <mark>When associated with malignancy, a tumor of intraabdominal origin—usually **gastric**—is seen in the majority of cases.</mark> <mark>It has been repeatedly described that patients' skin improves with chemotherapy and relapses with recurrence.</mark>

---

## Diabetic Thick Skin

<mark>Several specific syndromes are associated with localized thickening of the skin in diabetes.</mark> <mark>The common underlying pathogenesis involves biochemical alterations in dermal collagen and mucopolysaccharides.</mark> <mark>The clinical syndromes result from increased deposition and improper degradation of these constituents, likely related to the formation of **advanced glycation end products (AGEs)**.</mark>

---

## Limited Joint Mobility and Scleroderma-Like Syndrome

<mark>**Diabetic limited joint mobility (LJM)**, or **cheiroarthropathy**, presents as tightness and thickening of the skin and periarticular connective tissue of the fingers, resulting in a painless loss of joint mobility.</mark> <mark>Initial involvement typically begins at the distal interphalangeal joint of the fifth digit and progresses proximally to involve all fingers.</mark> <mark>Larger joints—such as those of the elbow, knee, and foot—may also be affected.</mark> <mark>However, the actual joint space remains uninvolved, so LJM is not a true arthropathy.</mark>

<mark>This disorder is characterized by the **"prayer sign"**, which is the inability to fully approximate the palmar surfaces and interphalangeal joint spaces when the hands are pressed together with fingers extended.</mark>

<mark>In addition to joint contractures, the skin may appear **thickened, waxy, and smooth**, with apparent loss of adnexal structures, resembling the skin changes seen in scleroderma.</mark>

LJM occurs in **30% to 50% of adult patients with type 1 diabetes** and is also common in type 2 diabetes. It is associated with **longer duration of diabetes** and **poor glycemic control**.

# <mark>CUTANEOUS DISORDERS OF DIABETES MELLITUS ASSOCIATED WITH METABOLIC, VASCULAR, NEUROLOGIC, OR IMMUNOLOGIC ABNORMALITIES</mark>

## <mark>Acanthosis Nigricans (See Chap. 154)</mark>

### <mark>EPIDEMIOLOGY</mark>  
Acanthosis nigricans is one of the most recognizable cutaneous manifestations of diabetes. <mark>It is common in the general population, with the majority of cases associated with obesity and insulin resistance.</mark> <mark>In some instances, increased androgen production may also contribute.[16,17] Drug-induced, idiopathic, and familial forms of acanthosis nigricans have been reported.[18]</mark>  

Acanthosis nigricans is considered a clinical marker for insulin resistance and a prognostic indicator for the development of type 2 diabetes.[19] In a large population-based study conducted in Galveston, Texas, acanthosis nigricans was present in 7% of school-aged children. <mark>This prevalence increased to 66% among children who weighed 200% of their ideal body weight.</mark> <mark>Fasting insulin levels in this cohort correlated directly with the presence and severity of skin changes.</mark>  

The prevalence of acanthosis nigricans varies across ethnic groups. In the Galveston study, despite similar obesity rates, the condition was less common in white children (0.5%) and Hispanic children (5%) compared to African American children (13%).[17] This suggests a possible genetic predisposition or increased cutaneous sensitivity to hyperinsulinemia in certain populations.[19]  

Although acanthosis nigricans has historically been linked to malignancy (particularly gastric adenocarcinoma), this association is rare. <mark>Evaluation for underlying malignancy is only warranted in cases with sudden onset, severe clinical presentation, or in non-obese, non-diabetic adults.</mark> Routine age-appropriate cancer screening is otherwise sufficient. In one clinician’s experience evaluating over 12,000 cancer patients, only two cases of acanthosis nigricans were observed.[20]

### ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS  
Insulin plays a central role in the development of acanthosis nigricans. Insulin resistance leads to hyperinsulinemia, which in turn stimulates insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) receptors in the skin. This cross-activation promotes keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation, resulting in the characteristic epidermal thickening, hyperpigmentation, and velvety texture of affected skin.  

Dysregulated lipid metabolism in insulin-deficient diabetes further contributes to cutaneous manifestations. Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity is insulin-dependent,[13] and its deficiency in uncontrolled diabetes impairs clearance of triglyceride-rich chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), leading to severe hypertriglyceridemia. This can manifest clinically as eruptive xanthomas.  

Macro- and microangiopathy are key contributors to diabetic skin complications. Diabetic microvasculature exhibits increased permeability, reduced responsiveness to sympathetic stimulation, and impaired adaptation to thermal and hypoxic stress.[10] These abnormalities, combined with large-vessel arteriosclerosis, predispose to poor wound healing and the development of diabetic foot ulcers.  

Additionally, peripheral sensory neuropathy results in loss of protective sensation, increasing the risk of trauma and infection. The disruption of neuroinflammatory signaling further impairs tissue repair, contributing to chronic, non-healing ulcers.[14] Patients with diabetes who lack vibratory perception in the lower extremities have a 15.5-fold higher risk of leg amputation.[15]  

Disorders of glucose and insulin signaling thus underlie a wide spectrum of cutaneous conditions through metabolic, vascular, neurologic, and immunologic mechanisms.

## Psoriasis Treatments and Comorbidities

### Metabolic Syndrome and Cardiovascular Risk

Systemic treatments for psoriasis are valuable not only for controlling skin symptoms but also for potentially improving aspects of metabolic syndrome, which is commonly associated with psoriasis. However, the impact of these treatments on metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors varies.

There is ongoing debate about whether newer therapies, particularly TNF inhibitors, lead to meaningful improvements in physiological markers of metabolic syndrome. Some studies suggest potential benefits, while others show neutral or even adverse effects. For example, weight gain has been observed in some patients using TNF inhibitors.[37]

Specific concerns include:
- **Cyclosporine**: May worsen atherogenic dyslipidaemia, arterial hypertension, and glucose intolerance.
- **Acitretin**: Can exacerbate atherogenic dyslipidaemia.
- **Methotrexate**: Requires caution in patients with increased risk of liver or renal toxicity.[38]

Therefore, careful monitoring and follow-up are recommended for patients receiving these therapies.

We also recommend increased surveillance for metabolic syndrome in psoriasis patients, including assessment of:
- Increasing waist circumference
- Elevated blood pressure
- Raised triglyceride levels
- Reduced HDL cholesterol
- Elevated fasting blood glucose

Additionally, patients should receive appropriate lifestyle interventions such as obesity management and smoking cessation counseling when indicated.

### Type II Diabetes and Insulin Resistance

<mark>From a safety standpoint, none of the available biological or non-biological systemic treatments for psoriasis are contraindicated in patients with type 2 diabetes or insulin resistance.</mark> <mark>However, clinical decision-making is limited by a lack of comparative data.</mark>

<mark>Some evidence suggests that anti-TNF agents—such as **infliximab**, **adalimumab**, **certolizumab pegol**, and **etanercept**—may reduce insulin resistance.[39–41] However, one study found no additional benefit of combining anti-TNF therapy with methotrexate over methotrexate alone in terms of HbA1c or fasting glucose levels.[42]</mark>

<mark>Other agents, including **methotrexate** and **acitretin**, have also been associated with improved insulin sensitivity in some studies.[43]</mark>

<mark>Caution is advised when using **cyclosporine** and **methotrexate** in diabetic patients due to increased risks of hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity.[38]</mark>

All systemic treatments currently available can be used in psoriasis patients with type 2 diabetes and/or insulin resistance. Recommended options include:
- **TNF antagonists**: adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, infliximab
- **IL-12/23 inhibitor**: ustekinumab
- **IL-23/p19 inhibitors**: guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab
- **IL-17 receptor blocker**: brodalumab
- **IL-17 inhibitors**: ixekizumab, secukinumab
- **Synthetic drug**: apremilast
- **Conventional drugs**: fumarates, acitretin

Cyclosporine and methotrexate may also be used, but with closer monitoring.

### Obesity in Psoriasis Patients

For obese patients with psoriasis, the following systemic treatments are recommended:
- **TNF antagonists**: adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept, infliximab
- **IL-12/23 inhibitor**: ustekinumab
- **IL-23/p19 inhibitors**: guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab
- **IL-17 receptor blocker**: brodalumab
- **IL-17 inhibitors**: ixekizumab, secukinumab
- **Synthetic drug**: apremilast
- **Conventional drugs**: fumarates, acitretin

Dietary interventions are encouraged, as they have been shown to improve outcomes with biologic therapy.[44]

From an efficacy perspective, studies indicate that certain biologics—**ustekinumab**, **infliximab**, **adalimumab**, and **etanercept**—as well as most conventional therapies, may require higher dosing in obese patients compared to those with healthy body weight.

Weight-adjusted dosing may therefore be necessary for optimal response in obese individuals. Currently, only **infliximab** and **ustekinumab** have established weight-based dosing regimens.[45,46] The need for dose adjustment with newer biologics remains less clear and requires further study.

# <mark>ACANTHOSIS NIGRICANS</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

<mark>Acanthosis nigricans is a cutaneous marker, most commonly of insulin resistance and less frequently of genetic disorders and malignancy.</mark>  
- <mark>Characterized by symmetric hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic, verrucous plaques that bestow a velvety texture on intertriginous skin and occasionally mucocutaneous areas.</mark>  
- <mark>Darker skin pigmentation, insulin resistance, and obesity are more commonly associated with benign acanthosis nigricans.</mark>  
- <mark>Malignant acanthosis nigricans often appears rapidly in older individuals and can involve atypical sites such as mucosal surfaces.</mark>

## ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

<mark>Although the precise etiology of benign acanthosis nigricans remains unclear, there is evidence that insulin plays a significant role.</mark> <mark>The pathogenesis of malignancy-associated acanthosis nigricans is even less clear.</mark> <mark>A humoral factor produced by the tumor is likely, given cases in which the skin disorder improved or resolved following treatment of the malignancy.</mark> <mark>Elevated urinary transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α) and increased expression of epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptors in lesional skin were noted in a patient with acanthosis nigricans, acrochordons, Leser-Trélat sign, and melanoma.</mark> <mark>The enhanced expression of this cytokine and its receptor normalized after removal of the melanoma, and the acanthosis nigricans, acrochordons, and seborrheic keratoses improved postoperatively.</mark> <mark>A separate case, with gastric cancer, was also shown to express TGF-α and EGF receptors.</mark>

<mark>More recently, a pathogenic role has been proposed for a tyrosine kinase receptor expressed on the basal cells of the epidermis.</mark> <mark>In several inherited human skeletal dysplasias associated with acanthosis nigricans, such as craniosynostoses and dwarfing chondrodysplasias, activating mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) can be observed, whereby FGFR3 has an inhibitory effect on bone formation.</mark> <mark>In other studies, FGFR3 has oncogenic effects in such malignancies as multiple myeloma, bladder, and cervical carcinoma.</mark> <mark>With respect to the role of FGFR3 on the epidermis, animal models with activating mutations develop benign epidermal tumors resembling acanthosis nigricans and seborrheic keratoses.</mark>

## <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

<mark>The clinical hallmark of acanthosis nigricans is development of gray-brown, velvety plaques that may start as a dirty appearance.</mark> <mark>The hyperpigmentation is later accompanied by hypertrophy, increased skin markings, and papillomatosis.</mark> <mark>Pruritus can be a problem in some patients.</mark> <mark>The most commonly involved locations are the axillae, neck, external genitalia, groin, face, inner thighs, antecubital and popliteal fossae, umbilicus, and perianal area.</mark> <mark>Acrochordons may develop, superimposed on the acanthosis nigricans or on other locations.</mark>

Dermatoses with high associations with internal malignancy include tripe palms, Bazex syndrome, paraneoplastic pemphigus, erythema gyratum repens, necrolytic migratory erythema, and hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita.  
<mark>Weakly associated with internal malignancy are acanthosis nigricans, acquired ichthyosis, and multiple seborrheic keratoses.</mark>  
Management of the dermatosis is the treatment of the malignancy.

Although reported in all age groups, at least 80 percent of malignancy-related acanthosis nigricans occurs in individuals over the age of 40 years.

## <mark>ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS</mark>

<mark>Advances are taking place in understanding the pathogenesis of acanthosis nigricans.</mark> <mark>Insulin clearly plays a central role in the presentation of acanthosis nigricans.</mark> In a subset of women with hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance with acanthosis nigricans, loss of function mutations in the insulin receptor or anti-insulin receptor antibodies can be found (Type A and Type B insulin resistance syndromes). <mark>It is postulated that excess growth factor stimulation in the skin causes the aberrant proliferation of keratinocytes and fibroblasts, resulting in the characteristic phenotype of acanthosis nigricans.</mark> <mark>In states of insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia, acanthosis nigricans may result from excess insulin binding to IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts.</mark> IGF-1 receptors are expressed on basal keratinocytes and are upregulated in proliferative skin conditions.

<mark>Studies show that high concentrations of insulin stimulate fibroblast proliferation through IGF-1 receptors in vitro.</mark> <mark>Other members of the tyrosine kinase receptor family, including the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR), have also been implicated in acanthosis nigricans.</mark> Several genetic syndromes—such as Crouzon syndrome and SADDAN (severe achondroplasia with developmental delay and acanthosis nigricans)—are caused by mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) and result in acanthosis nigricans in the absence of hyperinsulinemia or obesity, implicating this growth factor receptor in the disease’s pathogenesis. In cases of malignant acanthosis nigricans, transforming growth factor-α (TGF-α) released by tumor cells may stimulate keratinocyte proliferation via activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor.

Support for the role of various growth factors in the pathogenesis of acanthosis nigricans continues to grow.

<mark>In addition to direct effects of hyperinsulinemia on keratinocytes, insulin also appears to augment androgen levels in women.</mark> High insulin levels stimulate ovarian androgen production and can lead to ovarian hypertrophy with cystic changes. Although acanthosis nigricans is commonly associated with elevated androgens in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the skin lesions do not reliably respond to antiandrogen therapy, suggesting that hyperinsulinemia plays a more central role than hyperandrogenism in lesion development. Several drugs have also been reported to cause acanthosis nigricans, including systemic glucocorticoids, nicotinic acid, and estrogens such as diethylstilbestrol.

## CLINICAL FINDINGS: CUTANEOUS LESIONS

Clinically, acanthosis nigricans presents as brown to gray-black, papillomatous, hyperpigmented skin thickening in flexural areas, most commonly the posterolateral neck, axillae, groin, and abdominal folds. The distribution is typically symmetric. Affected skin has a velvety, "dirty" appearance. 

The back of the neck is the most consistently and severely affected site. Superimposed acrochordons (skin tags) frequently develop in involved areas. In more severe or florid cases, involvement may extend to the dorsal hands, knuckles, and even the palms, where a rugated (ridged) pattern may be observed.

Mucosal surfaces—including oral, esophageal, pharyngeal, laryngeal, conjunctival, and anogenital regions—can also be involved, though this is less common.

## <mark>Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH)</mark>

The reactive versus neoplastic nature of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) remains a subject of debate. <mark>However, the most probable hypothesis is that LCH arises from a clonal proliferation of histiocytes in genetically predisposed individuals.</mark>

### Histopathology
Histopathologic features of LCH include a dense infiltrate of histiocytes with prominent epidermotropism. The hallmark cell is the **"LCH cell"**—a histiocyte characterized by an irregular, vesiculated, often reniform (kidney-shaped) nucleus and abundant, slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. These cells are immunophenotypically positive for **S100 protein**, **CD1a**, and **CD207 (langerin)**, and contain cytoplasmic **Birbeck granules** (Langerhans granules).

### <mark>Clinical Features</mark>
Cutaneous manifestations of LCH are highly variable and may present as papules, vesicles, pustules, nodules, or ulcers. <mark>The disease course ranges from localized, self-healing forms to generalized, life-threatening presentations.</mark> Common sites of skin involvement include the **head, trunk, and skinfolds**. Mucosal lesions typically appear as **ulcerated nodules**, predominantly affecting the **gingiva** and **genital regions**.

### <mark>Systemic Involvement</mark>
LCH can involve multiple organ systems. <mark>Associated manifestations include:</mark>
- <mark>**Diabetes insipidus** (due to pituitary involvement)</mark>
- <mark>**Exophthalmos** (from orbital bone lesions)</mark>

<mark>Systemic organs that may be affected include:</mark>
- Bones
- Lungs
- Bone marrow
- Liver
- Spleen
- Lymph nodes

Aggressive forms of LCH can be treated with systemic chemotherapy, including **vinblastine** and other agents, with variable success.

### Disease Continuum and Classification
It is increasingly realistic to view LCH as a **clinical continuum**, as each patient presents uniquely in terms of lesion type, number, and location. While historical terminology persists for didactic use, the critical distinction lies in identifying:
- **Multisystem disease (extensive LCH)**: Requires systemic therapy
- **Single-system disease (restricted LCH)**: May be managed with topical treatment or observation
- **Self-healing forms**: Often resolve spontaneously

### Diagnostic Guidelines
The Writing Group of the Histiocyte Society has established confidence levels for the diagnosis of **Class I histiocytosis (LCH)**, emphasizing the importance of immunohistochemical and ultrastructural confirmation.

### Classification of Histiocytosis
**TABLE 148-1** Classification System for Histiocytosis (Histiocyte Society, 1987 and 2004)

- **Class I**: Langerhans cell histiocytosis  
- **Class II**: Non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis (mononuclear phagocyte system)
  - **IIa**: Histiocytosis involving dermal CD68+ and factor XIIIa+ dendrocytes
  - **IIb**: Histiocytosis involving cells other than Langerhans cells or dermal dendrocytes
- **Class III**: Malignant histiocytosis

This classification provides a framework for diagnosis and management, guiding therapeutic decisions based on disease extent and organ involvement.

# <mark>Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

A group of rare disorders that are considered reactive but have a broad spectrum of severity.  
<mark>The reactive versus neoplastic nature of LCH cells is debated.</mark> <mark>Although clonality has been demonstrated in all forms of LCH, this does not necessarily indicate malignant behavior.</mark> <mark>A clonal origin in genetically predisposed individuals is the most probable hypothesis.</mark>  
<mark>Histopathologic features consist of a dense infiltrate of histiocytes with strong epidermotropism.</mark> <mark>The unifying element is the typical "LCH cell"—a histiocyte with an irregular, vesiculated, often reniform nucleus and abundant, slightly eosinophilic cytoplasm.</mark> <mark>These cells are positive for S100 protein, CD1a, and CD207 (langerin), and contain cytoplasmic Birbeck granules.</mark>

## Pathogenesis

The nature of LCH—reactive versus neoplastic—remains controversial. Evidence supporting a **reactive hypothesis** includes:  
1. <mark>LCH cells are highly differentiated.</mark>  
2. <mark>Granulomatous lesions resemble those seen in infections or foreign-body reactions.</mark>  
3. <mark>Lesions may spontaneously regress.</mark>  

Proposed pathogenic steps in the reactive model:  
1. Viral infection induces activation of histiocytes.  
2. Immunologic mechanisms drive the pathologic Langerhans cell phenotype.  
3. A cytokine-mediated inflammatory storm leads to lesion formation.  

Numerous viruses—such as human herpesvirus 6, cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, and parvovirus—have been implicated in disease initiation, but none has been definitively proven as causative.

In contrast, evidence supporting a **clonal neoplastic origin** includes:  
1. <mark>Bone marrow origin and clonality of LCH cells.</mark>  
2. <mark>Rare familial cases of LCH.</mark>  
3. <mark>Chromosomal instability, including abnormalities on chromosome 7 and p53 protein overexpression.</mark>  
4. <mark>Co-occurrence of LCH and myelodysplastic syndrome.</mark>

Two explanations have been proposed for the association with myelodysplasia:  
- Marrow dysplasia may be secondary to cytokine-driven infiltration by LCH cells, rather than a true myelodysplastic syndrome.  
- Alternatively, both LCH and myelodysplastic cells may arise from a common clonal pluripotent dendritic (stem) cell, suggesting LCH could be classified as a "myeloid dendritic stem cell disorder."  

These findings imply a genetic predisposition and have prompted research into candidate genes involved in LCH pathogenesis.

## Clinical Findings

### Classification

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) presents across a wide clinical spectrum—from localized, asymptomatic disease to systemic, aggressive multisystem involvement. <mark>Clinical manifestations depend on the extent and location of lesions.</mark>

Historically, LCH has been categorized under several names based on clinical presentation:  
- **Letterer-Siwe disease (LSD):** Acute, disseminated, multisystem form typically affecting infants and newborns; untreated cases are often fatal.  
- **Hand-Schüller-Christian disease (HSC):** Chronic, progressive, multifocal form usually presenting in childhood.  
- **Eosinophilic granuloma (EG):** Localized, benign form, often limited to a single bone lesion.  
- **Hashimoto-Pritzker disease (HPD):** Self-healing, congenital variant presenting at birth or within the first days of life.

The Histiocyte Society has established a standardized classification system for histiocytoses (refer to Table 148-1).

# Saddle Nose Deformity

Saddle nose deformity is a characteristic feature of relapsing polychondritis (RP), resulting from inflammation and destruction of the nasal cartilage. This structural collapse can lead to upper airway compromise, obstructive respiratory insufficiency, and predispose to secondary infections. Costochondritis, occurring in approximately 35% of patients, causes parietal chest pain that may further impair respiration due to pain-related splinting.

## Musculoskeletal Involvement

Joint pain is a common presenting symptom in RP, affecting about 30% of patients. Involvement of both large and small joints of the peripheral and axial skeleton occurs in over 70% of cases. Arthritis in RP is typically intermittent, migratory, asymmetric, seronegative, and nonerosive.

## Ocular Manifestations

Ocular inflammation develops in nearly 60% of patients. The most frequent forms are episcleritis and scleritis, followed by keratoconjunctivitis sicca, iritis, retinopathy, and keratitis. Rare but severe complications—such as corneal perforation, retinal vasculitis, and optic neuritis—can result in blindness.

## Audiovestibular Involvement

Conductive hearing loss may arise from stenosis of the external auditory canal, eustachian tube chondritis, or serous otitis media. Sensorineural hearing loss can also occur due to inner ear involvement. Vestibular dysfunction may present acutely with dizziness, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting; symptoms often improve over time.

## Cardiovascular Manifestations

Cardiovascular involvement is diverse and potentially life-threatening. It may affect various cardiac structures, including:
- Aortic and/or mitral regurgitation
- Conduction system abnormalities
- Pericarditis

Vascular involvement includes:
- Thoracic and abdominal aortitis (may lead to aneurysms)
- Takayasu-like aortic arch syndrome
- Large and medium vessel vasculitis
- Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
- Thrombophlebitis

Lesions are primarily inflammatory or thrombotic. Some thrombotic events are associated with anti-phospholipid syndrome, though not all. Large vessel vasculitis often develops after years of subclinical disease activity, even during immunosuppressive therapy.

## Dermatologic Manifestations

Skin findings are the initial presentation in about 12% of RP cases and eventually appear in over one-third of patients. These are nonspecific and may include:
- Cutaneous nodules on the limbs
- Purpura
- Oral or complex aphthosis
- Papules and sterile pustules
- Superficial phlebitis
- Livedo reticularis
- Limb ulcerations
- Distal necrosis

These lesions may occur concurrently with or independently of chondritis episodes. Histopathology reveals inflammatory or thrombotic vascular changes, neutrophilic infiltrates resembling neutrophilic dermatoses, and dermal or subcutaneous inflammation.

While most patients with or without skin involvement have similar systemic manifestations, those with RP associated with myelodysplasia show a higher frequency of dermatologic features (>90%), earlier onset of chondritis, and a skewed male-to-female ratio.

# Laboratory Findings

## Histopathology

Histopathologic examination of affected cartilage demonstrates perichondrial inflammation and loss of normal basophilic staining of cartilage matrix, reflecting proteoglycan depletion.

## Other Laboratory Tests

Laboratory abnormalities in RP are nonspecific and reflect ongoing inflammation—either acute or chronic. Urinalysis may reveal abnormalities if renal involvement is present, such as:
- Mesangial expansion
- IgA nephropathy
- Tubulointerstitial nephritis
- Necrotizing glomerulonephritis

Pulmonary function tests, particularly inspiratory and expiratory flow-volume curves, should be performed routinely to detect subclinical respiratory tract involvement. Findings can be confirmed with computed tomography of the airways.

# Box 160-1: Empirical Diagnostic Criteria for Relapsing Polychondritis

- Bilateral auricular chondritis  
- Non-erosive seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis  
- Nasal chondritis  
- Ocular inflammation  
- Respiratory chondritis  
- Audiovestibular damage  

**Diagnostic Criteria:**  
A diagnosis of relapsing polychondritis requires one of the following:
- At least three of the above clinical criteria  
- One or more clinical criteria plus biopsy confirmation of cartilage inflammation  
- Chondritis at two or more separate anatomic sites with response to corticosteroids and/or dapsone  

*Data from Michet CJ et al: Relapsing polychondritis—Survival and predictive role of early disease manifestations. Ann Intern Med 104:74, 1986.*

<mark>Etiology of capillary malformations (CM) is currently unknown.</mark> <mark>Facial CM is thought to result from clonal expansion of abnormal cells originating from the neural crest.</mark> <mark>The identification of the affected gene (*RASA1*) in CM-AVM (see Arteriovenous Malformations) may provide insights into the pathogenesis of the more common sporadic CM.</mark>

<mark>Histologically, CM is characterized by dilatation of a normal number of capillaries in the papillary and upper reticular dermis, along with areas showing an increased number of otherwise normal-appearing capillaries (see Fig.</mark> 173-2). <mark>Endothelial cells are flat.</mark> <mark>Factor VIII, fibronectin, and basement membrane proteins are normal, but S100 staining reveals abnormal innervation.</mark>

# <mark>CAPILLARY MALFORMATIONS AT A GLANCE</mark>

- **Worldwide occurrence**: Affects approximately 0.1% to 0.2% of the population  
- **Type**: Congenital no-flow malformations of the capillary bed  
- **Color**: Pinkish-red to purple; tends to darken and thicken over time  
- **Clinical significance**: In most cases, a cosmetic concern  
- **Syndromic associations**: Can be part of Sturge-Weber syndrome, Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome, or phakomatosis pigmentovascularis  
- <mark>**Pathology**: Capillaries are increased in size and number, with evidence of abnormal innervation</mark>  

# Clinical Findings

## CUTANEOUS LESIONS (Fig. 173-3; See Fig. 173-2)

Capillary malformations (CM) present as red, homogenous, congenital lesions that are typically unilateral, occasionally bilateral, and rarely midline. They involve the skin and subcutis, and sometimes mucosa.  

- **Color**: Ranges from pinkish-red to deep purple  
- **Shape**: Geographic borders or dermatomal distribution  
- **Texture**: Flat, painless, non-blanching (under pressure), do not bleed spontaneously, and are not warm to touch  
- **Distribution**: Can occur anywhere on the body; 50% are located on the face, following the trigeminal nerve branches:
  - **V1 (ophthalmic)**: Forehead, upper eyelid  
  - **V2 (maxillary)**: Lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip  
  - **V3 (mandibular)**: Lower lip, chin, mandible  

CM may be associated with other vascular malformations as part of a syndrome, such as:
- **Sturge-Weber syndrome**
- **Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome**
- **Servelle-Martorell syndrome**
- **Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis**

These syndromes are not inherited.  

Rarely, CM in the lumbosacral region may be a cutaneous marker of occult spinal dysraphism.

# <mark>Clinical Findings of Herpes Zoster</mark>

## <mark>Prodrome of Herpes Zoster</mark>

<mark>Pain and paresthesia in the involved dermatome often precede the rash by several days, ranging from mild itching, tingling, or burning to severe, deep, boring, or lancinating pain.</mark> <mark>The pain may be constant or intermittent and is frequently associated with tenderness and hyperesthesia in the affected dermatome.</mark> 

Pre-eruptive pain can mimic conditions such as pleurisy, myocardial infarction, duodenal ulcer, cholecystitis, biliary or renal colic, appendicitis, prolapsed intervertebral disk, or early glaucoma, leading to potential misdiagnosis and inappropriate interventions. 

Prodromal pain is rare in immunocompetent individuals under 30 years of age but occurs in most patients over 60. Some patients experience acute segmental neuralgia without developing a skin rash—a condition termed **zoster sine herpete**.

## <mark>Rash of Herpes Zoster</mark>

<mark>The hallmark of herpes zoster is its unilateral distribution, typically confined to the skin area innervated by a single sensory ganglion.</mark> <mark>The rash most commonly affects the dermatomes supplied by the **trigeminal nerve** (especially the ophthalmic division) and the thoracic region (T3 to L2).</mark> <mark>The thoracic dermatomes account for over half of all cases, and lesions rarely extend beyond the elbows or knees.</mark>

<mark>Although individual lesions of herpes zoster and varicella are histologically identical, those in herpes zoster evolve more slowly and appear as **closely grouped vesicles on an erythematous base**, in contrast to the scattered, discrete vesicles seen in varicella.</mark> This pattern reflects **intraneural spread** of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in herpes zoster, as opposed to **hematogenous spread** in varicella.

Lesions begin as **erythematous macules and papules**, often appearing at sites where superficial sensory nerve branches emerge (e.g., posterior and lateral branches of spinal nerves). Vesicles develop within **12 to 24 hours**, progress to **pustules by day 3**, and then **dry and crust over within 7 to 10 days**. Crusts typically remain for **2 to 3 weeks**.

In immunocompetent individuals, new lesions appear for **1 to 4 days**, occasionally up to 7 days. The rash is most severe and prolonged in older adults and mildest and shortest in children.

The incidence and severity of fever are lower in herpes zoster compared to natural varicella.

# <mark>Immunosuppressive Conditions and Risk Factors for Herpes Zoster</mark>

Immunosuppressive conditions associated with high risk of herpes zoster include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, bone marrow transplant, leukemia and lymphoma, use of cancer chemotherapy, and use of corticosteroids. Herpes zoster is a prominent and early "opportunistic infection" in persons infected with HIV, in whom it is often the first sign of immune deficiency. Thus, HIV infection should be considered in individuals who develop herpes zoster.

Other factors reported to increase the risk of herpes zoster include female sex, physical trauma in the affected dermatome, interleukin-10 gene polymorphisms, and black race, but confirmation is required. Exposure to children and contact with cases of varicella have been reported to confer protection against herpes zoster.

Second episodes of herpes zoster are uncommon in immunocompetent persons, and third attacks are very rare. Persons suffering more than one episode may be immunocompromised. Immunocompetent patients suffering multiple episodes of herpes zoster-like disease are likely to be suffering from recurrent zosteriform herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections.

# Contagiousness and Transmission

Patients with herpes zoster are less contagious than patients with varicella. The rate at which susceptible household contacts develop varicella after exposure to herpes zoster appears to be about one-third of the rate observed after exposure to varicella. Virus can be isolated from vesicles and pustules in uncomplicated herpes zoster for up to 7 days after the appearance of the rash, and for much longer periods in immunocompromised individuals.

Patients with uncomplicated dermatomal zoster appear to spread the infection by means of direct contact with their lesions. Patients with disseminated herpes zoster may, in addition, transmit the infection via aerosols, so that airborne precautions, as well as contact precautions, are required for such patients.

# Impact of Varicella Vaccination on Herpes Zoster Epidemiology

The effect of the marked reduction in the incidence of varicella, due to widespread varicella vaccination of children, on the epidemiology of herpes zoster is unclear. In the long term, the incidence of herpes zoster is likely to decline as the cohorts of children now receiving the vaccine become adults; vaccine virus-associated herpes zoster will probably be less frequent and less severe in older adults than wild-type virus-associated herpes zoster because the vaccine virus is highly attenuated.

In the short term, the incidence of herpes zoster could increase because a decline in the incidence of varicella will reduce the adult population's exposure to VZV, thereby reducing immune boosting, hastening the age-related decline in immunity to VZV, and thus increasing the age-specific risk of herpes zoster. However, recent studies of herpes zoster in populations with high rates of varicella vaccination have shown little or no increase in the incidence of herpes zoster.

# <mark>ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS</mark>

Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a member of the herpesvirus family. Other members pathogenic for humans include herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and type 2 (HSV-2), cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) and HHV-7 (which cause roseola), and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (also called HHV-8). All herpesviruses are morphologically indistinguishable and share key properties, including the ability to establish latent infections that persist for life.

The VZV genome encodes approximately 70 unique genes, most of which have DNA sequence and functional homology to genes of other herpesviruses. Immediate-early gene products regulate VZV replication. Early gene products, such as the virus-specific thymidine kinase and the viral DNA polymerase, support viral replication. Late genes encode structural proteins of the virus that serve as targets for antibody and cellular immune responses.

There is only one VZV serotype. Although viruses isolated from individual cases of varicella or herpes zoster worldwide are fundamentally similar, minor variations in their nucleotide sequences allow differentiation between wild-type and vaccine virus strains and enable "fingerprinting" of viruses from individual patients.

## Pathogenesis of Varicella

VZV enters through the mucosa of the upper respiratory tract and oropharynx. Initial viral replication at this site leads to primary viremia, with dissemination of small amounts of virus via the blood and lymphatics. This virus is then cleared by cells of the reticuloendothelial system, which become the major site of viral replication during the remainder of the incubation period.

## <mark>HERPES ZOSTER IN THE IMMUNOCOMPROMISED HOST</mark>

<mark>Except for postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), most serious complications of herpes zoster occur in immunocompromised individuals.</mark> <mark>These complications include skin necrosis and scarring, as well as cutaneous dissemination, which occurs in 25% to 50% of such patients.</mark> <mark>Approximately 10% of those with cutaneous dissemination develop widespread, often fatal, visceral involvement affecting the lungs, liver, and brain.</mark>

<mark>HIV-infected patients are particularly prone to multiple recurrences of herpes zoster as their disease progresses.</mark> <mark>Recurrences may involve the same or different dermatomes, including contiguous or non-contiguous ones.</mark> <mark>In patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), herpes zoster can be severe, with cutaneous and visceral dissemination.</mark> <mark>Additionally, these patients may develop chronic verrucous, hyperkeratotic, or ecthymatous skin lesions due to acyclovir-resistant varicella-zoster virus (VZV).</mark>

---

## DIAGNOSIS OF VARICELLA

Varicella is typically diagnosed based on the characteristic appearance and progression of the rash (see Fig. 194-4), especially when there is a history of exposure within the preceding 2 to 3 weeks.

Disseminated herpes zoster may mimic varicella when VZV spreads widely from a small, painless zoster lesion or from an affected sensory ganglion, even in the absence of a clear dermatomal rash. This presentation is not uncommon in profoundly immunosuppressed, VZV-seropositive individuals.

Disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections can also resemble varicella; however, lesions are typically concentrated around the site of primary or recurrent infection (e.g., mouth or genitalia), and patients may exhibit significant systemic toxicity or encephalitis.

The differential diagnoses of varicelliform rashes are listed in Box 194-1. The morphology, distribution, and evolution of lesions, along with a detailed epidemiologic history, usually allow differentiation from varicella. When diagnostic uncertainty persists, laboratory confirmation should be obtained.

---

## DIAGNOSIS OF HERPES ZOSTER

In the pre-eruptive phase, the prodromal pain of herpes zoster is often mistaken for other causes of localized pain. Once the rash appears, the characteristic dermatomal distribution, along with associated dermatomal pain or discomfort, typically makes the diagnosis clinically evident (see Figs. 194-5 and 194-6).
