# <mark>Clinical Features of Raynaud Phenomenon</mark>

<mark>During attacks, one or more fingers or toes may become numb and feel "dead." Upon re-warming, the affected digits often turn bright red and may be accompanied by throbbing pain.</mark> <mark>When pain is prominent during the ischemic phase, a secondary cause should be suspected.</mark> <mark>Episodes typically last from minutes to hours.</mark> <mark>The fingers and toes are most commonly affected, though the nose, earlobes, and nipples can also be involved.</mark>

<mark>A thorough review of systems is essential to evaluate for underlying conditions.</mark> <mark>Screen for symptoms suggestive of connective tissue disease (e.g., arthralgias, arthritis, dysphagia, heartburn, rash, photosensitivity, skin changes, muscle weakness, shortness of breath, sicca symptoms), drug-induced causes, signs of obstructive arterial disease (such as intermittent claudication), and exposure to vibratory tools or repetitive finger trauma.</mark>

## Cutaneous Lesions

<mark>Stress-induced attacks of Raynaud phenomenon are often observed during the patient interview or physical examination.</mark> <mark>Characteristic findings include well-demarcated blanching or cyanosis extending from the tip of the digit proximally.</mark> <mark>The skin distal to the ischemic line is cold, while the proximal skin remains pink and warm.</mark> <mark>With re-warming, blanched areas may first become cyanotic due to sluggish blood flow, then turn bright red as reactive hyperemia occurs.</mark> <mark>Persistent ischemic discoloration suggests a secondary cause.</mark>

<mark>Careful inspection of the digits should assess for trophic or ischemic changes, which indicate chronic or severe disease.</mark> <mark>Skin may appear atrophic, thin, and tight—termed **sclerodactyly**—with loss of dorsal hair.</mark> <mark>Nails may become brittle and malformed.</mark> <mark>Painful ulcerations can develop on the finger pads or around the nail folds, often worsening at night.</mark> <mark>These ulcers heal slowly, may become infected, and typically leave small, pitted scars.</mark> <mark>Digital gangrene is rare but possible in advanced cases.</mark>

## Related Physical Findings

The physical examination should include assessment of all peripheral pulses and bilateral arm blood pressure measurements. **Allen’s test** is useful for evaluating arterial inflow to the hands; abnormal results suggest structural microvascular disease and raise concern for secondary Raynaud phenomenon.

To perform Allen’s test:
- Compress both the radial and ulnar arteries while the patient opens and closes the fist until the palm blanches.
- Release pressure on one artery at a time and observe the speed of color return, indicating adequacy of arterial supply.

Assess for vascular obstruction due to **thoracic outlet syndrome** using the **Adson maneuver**: evaluate for diminished radial pulse with neck extension and rotation or arm abduction.

A detailed neurologic examination should be performed to detect signs of sympathetic hyperactivity, abnormal reflexes, muscle weakness or atrophy, or **carpal tunnel syndrome** (median nerve compression).

Skin examination may reveal **telangiectases**, abnormal skin texture, rashes, or **purpura**, which can provide clues to underlying connective tissue disease or hyperviscosity syndromes.

Nail fold capillary microscopy may show **capillary dropout**, along with enlarged, dilated, and tortuous capillary loops—commonly seen in scleroderma (Fig. 171-3).

# Organ involvement and diagnostic work-up

## <mark>Raynaud's phenomenon</mark>

<mark>Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by vasospasm leading to a triphasic color change: blanching (pallor), cyanosis, and reactive hyperemia.</mark> <mark>It is present in more than 90% of patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc).</mark> <mark>It most commonly affects the hands, less frequently the feet, and may also involve the tongue, ears, and nose.</mark> <mark>Typical triggers include cold exposure and emotional stress.</mark>

<mark>Primary Raynaud's phenomenon is primarily due to functional vascular dysregulation, whereas secondary Raynaud's phenomenon—particularly in the context of SSc—involves both functional abnormalities and structural changes in the digital arteries.</mark> <mark>These structural alterations contribute significantly to the development of digital ulcers.</mark>

<mark>Differentiating between primary and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon requires nailfold capillaroscopy and autoantibody analysis.</mark> <mark>Additional laboratory and imaging studies may be necessary to rule out other underlying causes.</mark>

<mark>The presence of clinical or laboratory features suggestive of connective tissue disease in patients with Raynaud's phenomenon increases the risk of progression to systemic sclerosis or a related disorder.</mark> <mark>This concept has been formalized in the Very Early Diagnosis of Systemic Sclerosis (VEDOSS) criteria, which help identify high-risk individuals for early intervention and monitoring.</mark>

## Skin fibrosis

At disease onset, especially in the diffuse cutaneous form of SSc, patients often present with swollen fingers and hands—commonly referred to as "puffy hands." This is followed by progressive skin thickening, leading to sclerodactyly, joint contractures, and functional impairment.

Characteristic facial changes include perioral pitting (radial furrowing around the mouth), microstomia (reduced mouth opening), and a mask-like facial appearance due to skin tightening.

The modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS) is the gold standard for assessing skin fibrosis. It evaluates skin thickness at 17 body sites through manual palpation. Each site is scored from 0 to 3:
- 0: normal skin
- 1: mild thickening
- 2: moderate thickening
- 3: severe thickening

The total score is the sum of all individual scores. The mRSS is reliable, validated, and widely used for both initial assessment and monitoring disease progression. Proper training is essential for accurate and consistent application.

Other tools such as ultrasound, MRI, and durometry have been explored in research settings but are not validated for routine clinical use and have not demonstrated superiority over mRSS in clinical trials.

Skin fibrosis severity often correlates with internal organ involvement, particularly early in the disease. However, in later stages, skin thickening may stabilize or improve while visceral organ involvement (e.g., lung, heart, kidney) progresses.

Additional cutaneous manifestations of fibrosis include alopecia, reduced sweating (hypohidrosis), hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, and severe pruritus.

## Digital ulceration

Digital ulcers (DUs) are a common and debilitating complication of SSc, affecting 15–25% of patients at any given time, with up to 35% experiencing them during the course of their disease. Prevalence varies across centers and studies.

Risk factors for DUs include:
- Extent of skin sclerosis
- Male sex
- Pulmonary arterial hypertension
- Esophageal involvement
- Presence of anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibodies (but not anti-centromere antibodies)
- Early onset of Raynaud’s phenomenon
- Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)

A history of digital ulcers at initial presentation is a strong predictor of future ulcer development and is associated with increased cardiovascular complications and reduced survival.

Ulcers over the extensor surfaces of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints have a multifactorial etiology, resulting from a combination of:
- Ischemia due to microvascular disease
- Mechanical stress on tight, fibrotic skin
- Minor trauma

Complications of digital ulcers include secondary infection, osteomyelitis, gangrene, and, in severe cases, amputation. Acroosteolysis—resorption of the distal phalanges—can further impair wound healing and contribute to chronicity.

# <mark>Secondary Raynaud Phenomenon</mark>

## <mark>Connective Tissue Disease</mark>
- <mark>**Scleroderma**: 80% to 90% of patients manifest Raynaud phenomenon or persistent vasospasm. It is the presenting symptom in about one-third of cases and may be the sole manifestation for years.</mark>
- **Systemic lupus erythematosus**: Raynaud phenomenon occurs in approximately one-third of patients.
- <mark>**Dermatomyositis and polymyositis**: Also associated with Raynaud phenomenon in about one-third of cases.</mark>
- <mark>**Undifferentiated connective tissue disease**</mark>
- **Systemic vasculitis**
- <mark>**Sjögren syndrome**</mark>
- <mark>**Eosinophilic fasciitis**</mark>

Arteriograms in connective tissue diseases often reveal obstructions in digital arteries, and sometimes in ulnar or radial arteries.

## Occupational and Environmental Exposure
- **Vibration-induced injury**: Common in workers using vibratory tools (e.g., air hammers, chain saws, rivet guns). Prevalence can reach up to 90% in high-risk occupations such as logging or mining.
- **Cold exposure**: Seen in occupations involving prolonged cold exposure (e.g., butchers, ice cream workers, fish packers).
- **Post-traumatic injury**: Includes hypothenar hammer syndrome and crutch-induced vascular injury.
- **Vinyl chloride disease**
- **Cold injury**

## Neurologic Disorders
Any neurologic condition causing permanent limb disuse may lead to sympathetic nervous system dysfunction, resulting in:
- Persistent vasospasm
- Coldness, pallor, or cyanosis
- Ulcerations
- Raynaud phenomenon

<mark>Conditions include:</mark>
- **Carpal tunnel syndrome**: Raynaud phenomenon often affects the first, index, and middle fingers (median nerve distribution).
- **Reflex sympathetic dystrophy**: Thermoregulatory abnormalities are a prominent feature.
- **Hemiplegia**
- **Polio**
- **Multiple sclerosis**
- **Syringomyelia**
- Nerve root compression or entrapment

Neurovascular compression at the **thoracic outlet** (e.g., due to cervical ribs, scalenus anticus abnormalities, bony deformities, or shoulder syndromes like costoclavicular or hyperabduction syndrome) can also cause Raynaud phenomenon.

## Drugs and Toxins
Medications and substances associated with Raynaud phenomenon include:
- **β-Adrenergic blockers** (e.g., propranolol) – commonly implicated in cardiovascular and migraine treatment
- **Ergotamines** and **methysergide** – used for migraines; can induce vasospasm
- **Oral contraceptives**
- **Clonidine**
- **Bromocriptine**
- **Cyclosporine**
- **Amphetamines**
- **Fluoxetine**
- **Interferon-α**
- **Bleomycin** and **vinblastine**

## Obstructive Arterial Disease
- **Atherosclerosis**
- **Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)**
- **Thromboembolism**
- **Thoracic outlet syndrome**

## Hyperviscosity Disorders
- **Cryoproteins**
- **Cold agglutinins**
- **Macroglobulins** (e.g., Waldenström macroglobulinemia)
- **Polycythemia**
- **Thrombocytosis**

## Miscellaneous
- **Hypothyroidism**
- **Infections**: Bacterial endocarditis, Lyme disease, viral hepatitis
- **Neoplasms**
- **Primary pulmonary hypertension**
- **Arteriovenous fistula**
- **Intra-arterial injections**

# Diagnostic procedures

## <mark>Clinical presentation and physical examination</mark>

<mark>The diagnosis of systemic sclerosis (SSc) is challenging due to the heterogeneity of disease manifestations and variable disease course.</mark> In 1980, the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) published preliminary classification criteria for patients with established disease. A subclassification developed by LeRoy et al. has become the most widely used system in clinical practice and serves as the foundation for many global registries (Table 3).

<mark>It is now widely accepted that **CREST syndrome** (calcinosis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) and **systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma** fall within the spectrum of **limited cutaneous SSc**.</mark>

For patients with very early disease—also referred to as very early/early SSc, pre-SSc, or undifferentiated connective tissue disease—there are no universally accepted diagnostic criteria. <mark>Among individuals presenting with **Raynaud’s phenomenon**, **nail fold capillaroscopic abnormalities**, and/or **SSc-specific autoantibodies** (e.g., anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase-1), approximately two-thirds will develop definite SSc within 5 years, and nearly **80%** will progress to definite disease over the long term.</mark> In contrast, those without a scleroderma pattern on capillaroscopy or SSc-specific antibodies have a very low risk of progression to SSc (**1.8%** during long-term follow-up).

## Skin manifestations

<mark>**Raynaud’s phenomenon** is present in more than **90%** of patients with SSc.</mark> <mark>It most commonly affects the hands, less frequently the feet, and may also involve the tongue, ears, and nose.</mark> <mark>Typical triggers include cold exposure and emotional stress.</mark>

<mark>At disease onset—particularly in the diffuse cutaneous form—patients often experience prolonged swelling of the fingers and hands ("**puffy hands**").</mark> <mark>This is followed by progressive skin thickening (sclerosis), leading to **sclerodactyly**, **dermatogenic contractures**, **perioral plication**, **microstomia**, and a **mask-like facial appearance**.</mark>

<mark>Additional cutaneous features may include:</mark>
- <mark>Hair loss</mark>
- <mark>Reduced sweating (hypohidrosis)</mark>
- <mark>Hyperpigmentation or depigmentation</mark>
- <mark>Severe pruritus</mark>

<mark>In later stages, skin fibrosis of the trunk and proximal extremities may stabilize or even improve, while internal organ involvement can progress.</mark>

<mark>Digital ulcers are a common complication:</mark>
- <mark>**15–25%** of SSc patients have active digital ulcers</mark>
- <mark>**Approximately 35%** have current or a history of digital ulcers (rates vary across centers)</mark>

<mark>Fingertip ulcers are typically ischemic in origin, whereas ulcers over the extensor surfaces of the interphalangeal joints result from a combination of poor perfusion, taut fibrotic skin, and trauma.</mark> <mark>Complications of digital ulcers include:</mark>
- <mark>Secondary infection</mark>
- <mark>Osteomyelitis</mark>
- <mark>Acro-osteolysis</mark>
- <mark>Gangrene</mark>

<mark>**Calcinosis cutis**—deposits of calcium carbonate in the subcutaneous tissue—occurs in all SSc subtypes and predominantly affects acral areas (fingers, elbows, knees).</mark> <mark>These deposits may cause pain, skin erosion, and ulceration.</mark>

## Musculoskeletal manifestations

**Arthralgia** and **musculoskeletal pain** are among the most common complaints in SSc and may contribute to secondary **fibromyalgia**.

**Tendon friction rubs**, heard on auscultation over tendons (especially in the hands), are a characteristic sign of active inflammation and are associated with more progressive disease.

**Muscle weakness** and mild elevations in **serum creatine kinase (CK)** levels are relatively common and may suggest an **SSc-myositis overlap syndrome**.

**Inflammatory arthritis** occurs in up to **10%** of patients and should raise suspicion for an **SSc–rheumatoid arthritis overlap syndrome**.

## Pulmonary manifestations

**Interstitial lung disease (ILD)** affects up to **65%** of SSc patients, with varying degrees of severity. The typical radiological pattern is **bibasilar** and most commonly corresponds to **non-specific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP)**.

**High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT)** of the chest is more sensitive than pulmonary function tests in detecting early ILD and is considered essential in the evaluation of SSc-related lung involvement.

# <mark>Physical Examination</mark>

<mark>All pressure ulcer patients should undergo a full physical examination to identify systemic diseases contributing to wound development, such as anemia, chronic cardiac or respiratory disease, and neurologic disorders.</mark>

# <mark>Ulcer Evaluation</mark>

Staging is an assessment system that classifies pressure ulcers based on the anatomic depth of soft-tissue damage. <mark>Pressure ulcers often progress from lower to higher stages, and any small pressure ulcer should be considered the possible "tip of an iceberg." Palpation is important to assist visual evaluation, and debridement is often necessary to determine the true extent of ulceration.</mark> <mark>Ulcers that initially appear superficial may be classified as stage III or IV after debridement reveals deeper tissue involvement.</mark> The epidermis may show hypertrophy at the ulcer margin with varying degrees of pigmentation.

Several staging systems are used to classify pressure ulcers. The most commonly used include the National Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel (NPUAP), Shea, and Yarkony and Kirk systems. These systems differ in criteria and categorization but aim to standardize assessment and guide treatment.

# Related Physical Findings

Tenderness, erythema, edema, warmth of surrounding skin, exudate, and foul odor are signs of local infection. Fever, along with declining mental or physical status, should raise suspicion for bacteremia or osteomyelitis.

Spasticity resulting from inflammation or infection may lead to muscle contractures and joint deformities, limiting mobility and complicating patient positioning. Weakness, anemia, and dehydration may also be present due to significant fluid and protein loss from chronic, draining wounds.

# Clinical Findings

## History

A thorough history and physical examination for pressure ulcer patients should include the use of a validated risk assessment scale. The Braden, Waterlow, and Norton scales are the most widely used tools for predicting the risk of developing pressure ulcers. These scales have been extensively tested for reliability and validity and are recommended by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. Key risk factors assessed include:

- Mobility
- Activity
- Moisture exposure
- Nutritional status
- Friction and shear
- Sensory perception

# Laboratory Tests

The diagnosis of pressure ulcers is primarily clinical. However, laboratory abnormalities such as anemia, leukocytosis, hypoproteinemia, or low serum iron levels may be present and reflect underlying systemic compromise. It is important to rule out other conditions that can cause skin ulcers, including calciphylaxis, vasculitis, and connective tissue diseases.

# Biopsy

Histologic analysis can be useful when clinical evaluation is insufficient to determine ulcer depth or to exclude other ulcerative conditions. In chronic pressure ulcers, there is a risk of malignant transformation, particularly to squamous cell carcinoma, known as Marjolin’s ulcer. Histopathologic findings in pressure ulcers are detailed in relevant clinical tables.

# Imaging Studies

Imaging is most valuable for identifying complications of deep pressure ulcers. 

- **Plain radiographs** can detect ectopic bone, gas in the ulcer cavity (suggesting infection), and sclerotic or destructive changes in underlying bone.
- Ectopic bone formation may contribute to ulcer development by altering posture and increasing localized pressure.
- When the extent of deep tissue involvement is unclear, **sinography** may be performed to delineate sinus tracts or fistulous connections.

# <mark>TREATMENT</mark>

<mark>Therapy should be individualized for each patient and involves more than simple wound management.</mark> <mark>Pressure ulcers are frequently a clinical sign of underlying medical conditions that should be treated to facilitate healing.</mark> Few controlled trials have evaluated specific treatment modalities for pressure ulcers. The general principles of therapy for pressure ulcers are the following.

## <mark>Relief of Pressure, Shear, and Frictional Forces</mark>

### <mark>POSITIONING</mark>

<mark>Positioning techniques are critical in the management of tissue loads.</mark>

<mark>While in bed, patients should be positioned to avoid pressure over existing ulcers or over bony prominences, especially the trochanter.</mark> <mark>Pillows or foam wedges can be used to lift a pressure ulcer off its support surface or to prevent direct contact between bony prominences, such as knees or ankles.</mark> <mark>It is important to limit the amount of time the head of the bed is elevated and to maintain the head of the bed at the lowest possible level of elevation tolerable to reduce shearing forces at sacral tissues.</mark> <mark>Immobilized patients are usually placed in a $30^{\circ}$ oblique position to the left or right, which should be alternated every 2 hours at a minimum.</mark>

The patient and caregivers must learn appropriate transfer or mobilization techniques to avoid friction. The patient should be lifted rather than dragged across the bedsheets, using lifting devices such as a trapeze or bed linen. <mark>Repositioning should be done as frequently as warranted by the patient's condition.</mark>

Moisture from urinary or fecal incontinence, perspiration, or wound drainage should be minimized, and the skin should be kept clean. Absorbent underpads, briefs, diapers, and occasionally urinary catheters or rectal tubes may be required to help manage incontinence. Skin barrier creams can help protect the skin from maceration.

Patients who are sitting may select a pressure-relieving cushion based on specific needs. Donut-type devices should be avoided because they result in venous congestion and may worsen ulcers. Patients should be encouraged to reposition themselves frequently.

### SUPPORT SURFACES

Support surfaces can be used on top of or instead of standard mattresses.

# Pain Management

<mark>Pain management requires a combination of conservative measures, medications, and appropriate wound care.</mark> <mark>Muscle relaxants and physical and occupational therapy may be helpful to decrease muscle spasm in the area of ulceration.</mark> <mark>Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation may help relieve acute and chronic pain.</mark> <mark>The use of topical anesthetics such as lidocaine-prilocaine cream on wounds 30 minutes before débridement significantly reduces pain associated with wound care procedures.</mark>

Nonopioid analgesics (aspirin, other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) are first-line systemic therapy, followed by stronger medications such as opioids. Adjuvant medications such as tricyclic antidepressants can be used to enhance analgesia. They can also improve depression in some chronic pain states and have sedative, sleep-enhancing qualities.

# Nutritional Management

Screening for nutritional deficiencies is an important part of assessment and management of pressure ulcers. Adequate patient dietary intake of protein is important in healing pressure ulcers. A reasonable protein amount is between 1.2 and $1.5\,\mathrm{g/kg/day}$, and caloric intake should be between 30 and $35\,\mathrm{kcal/kg/day}$. Vitamin C or zinc deficiency can have negative effects on wound healing, but supplementation is useful only when deficiency is confirmed or suspected. If dietary intake continues to be inadequate, oral or parenteral nutritional supplementation may be required. Markers of nutritional deficiency include a serum albumin level of less than $3.5\,\mathrm{mg/dL}$ and unintentional weight loss of more than 15 percent of baseline. Patients should be kept adequately hydrated.

# Surgery

The long-term efficacy of surgical repair of pressure ulcers, especially in older patients, has been questioned because of high recurrence rates and mortality. The decision to undertake surgical repair should be made with full knowledge of the risks and benefits, surgical and nonsurgical alternatives, and complications associated with each procedure. Surgical techniques include skin grafting; creation of cutaneous, muscle, and fasciocutaneous flaps or pedicled flaps; microvascular free tissue transfer reconstruction; and simple direct suture, depending on the site, number, and grade of lesions, and the patient's clinical condition. In general, surgery is often required for stage IV ulcers, whereas more superficial ulcers may heal with conservative therapy.

# Adjunctive Therapies

Adjunctive therapies have been used in case studies, but more data are needed to determine the effectiveness of these therapies. These therapies are outlined in the electronic version of this book.

Whenever possible, other factors that impair healing—such as smoking, hypovolemia, cold exposure, chronic diseases (including diabetes mellitus, systemic arterial hypertension, anemia, and vascular alterations), and the use of medications such as corticosteroids—should be limited or controlled.

# Prevention

Preventive actions can decrease the patient's risk of developing pressure ulcers. These steps can also keep pressure ulcers from getting worse. Preventive measures are listed in Table 99-6.

## TABLE 99-6 Preventive Measures

- Maintain personal hygiene.  
- Assure adequate nutrition and hydration.  
- Evaluate and manage urinary and fecal incontinence.  
- Position to alleviate pressure over bony prominences and shearing forces over heels, elbows, base of head, and ears.  
- Reposition every 2 hours when in bed and every hour when in a chair; if alert and capable, the patient should be taught to shift weight every 15 minutes while in a chair.  
- Use appropriate positioning devices and foam padding; do not use donut-shaped devices.  
- Avoid placing the patient on the trochanters or directly on the wound.  
- Maintain the lowest head elevation possible.  
- Use lifting devices such as draw sheets or a trapeze.  
- Prevent contractures.  
- Do not massage reddened areas over bony prominences.

## <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

Childhood is marked by periods of significant and rapid growth and development, and nutritional deprivation often manifests as alterations in these patterns. <mark>**Failure to thrive**, a key finding in patients with **protein-energy malnutrition (PEM)**, may appear first as **wasting** (poor weight gain or weight loss), and eventually progress to **stunting** (decreased linear growth).</mark>  

Recommended markers for malnutrition include:
- Body weight and length/height relative to age  
- Body mass index (BMI)  
- Triceps or mid-upper arm circumference  
- Skin and hair characteristics  

Chronically malnourished children may also exhibit:
- Suboptimal neurodevelopmental outcomes  
- Increased susceptibility to infections  
- Elevated risk of mortality  

### Marasmus

Marasmus typically affects infants younger than 1 year of age. Physical findings include:
- **Dry, thin, loose, wrinkled skin** due to loss of subcutaneous fat, resulting in an emaciated appearance  
- **Slowed hair growth**, easy hair loss, leading to thin, fine, brittle hair and **alopecia**  
- Presence of **increased lanugo hair**  
- **Nail fissuring** and impaired nail growth  

As the body utilizes all available energy stores:
- Loss of **subcutaneous fat** and **muscle mass** occurs  
- Loss of **buccal fat pads** leads to a characteristic aged or "wizened" facial appearance, historically termed **"monkey facies"**  
- **Perianal fat loss** may result in **rectal prolapse**  
- **Abdominal muscle hypotonia** can cause **abdominal distention**  

Gastrointestinal symptoms include:
- Alternating **constipation** and **diarrhea**, with or without concurrent gastrointestinal infection  
- **Angular cheilitis** and mucous membrane changes  

Additional clinical features:
- **Decreased resting body temperature**  
- **Bradycardia**  

### <mark>Kwashiorkor</mark>

<mark>Kwashiorkor, also known as **edematous** or **"wet" PEM**, is characterized by:</mark>
- <mark>**Failure to thrive**</mark>  
- <mark>**Edema** (typically starting in the lower extremities and progressing to generalized swelling)</mark>  
- <mark>Typically affects children between **6 months and 5 years of age**</mark>  

<mark>Behavioral changes:</mark>
- <mark>Initial **irritability**, progressing to **lethargy** and **apathy**</mark>  

<mark>Dermatologic manifestations:</mark>
- <mark>**"Flaky paint" or "crazy pavement" dermatosis**: areas of hyperpigmentation with desquamation and fissuring, resembling cracked paint or pavement</mark>  
- **Hyperpigmentation** on extensor surfaces of arms and legs  

Hair changes:
- Early stage: hair develops a **red or reddish tint**  
- Later stage: **pigment loss** leads to **light, gray-white hair**  

Hypoproteinemia, edema, and diarrhea are prominent. Patients are unable to synthesize lipoproteins, leading to **fat accumulation in the liver** (hepatic steatosis). Critically, **immune proteins are not produced**, resulting in **increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections and septicemia**, which are major causes of mortality.  

The exact reason why some children develop **marasmus** versus **kwashiorkor** under conditions of starvation remains controversial, despite the conceptual frameworks of adapted and nonadapted starvation.

# <mark>Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)</mark>

The United Nations estimates that 852 million individuals, including approximately 170 million—about a quarter of the world's children—suffer from protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), with up to 5 million deaths annually attributed to PEM alone.

<mark>In developing countries, malnutrition most commonly results from inadequate dietary intake, often exacerbated by disease.</mark> <mark>Factors such as war, famine, poverty, political unrest, natural disasters, infectious diseases, seasonal and climatic variations, insufficient food production, lack of education, poor sanitation, regional and religious practices, and limited access to health care further restrict food availability.</mark> In contrast, in Western industrialized nations like the United States, less than 1% of children suffer from PEM. When it does occur, it is typically associated with chronic illness, malabsorption, presumed food allergies, nutritional ignorance, or adherence to fad diets.

## Etiology and Pathogenesis

<mark>Protein-energy malnutrition refers to a spectrum of disorders caused by varying degrees of protein and calorie deficiency.</mark> <mark>Several subtypes of PEM are defined based on the relative deficiencies in protein and total caloric intake.</mark>

### <mark>Marasmus</mark>
<mark>Children with marasmus experience severe wasting and stunting, with body weight below 60% of the expected weight for age.</mark> <mark>The term "marasmus" comes from the Greek *marasmos*, meaning "wasting." This condition results from chronic, generalized nutrient deficiency, often due to prolonged food scarcity.</mark>

### <mark>Kwashiorkor</mark>
<mark>Children with kwashiorkor typically have body weights between 60% and 80% of expected for age.</mark> <mark>It generally arises from a diet high in carbohydrates—such as grain-based foods—but deficient in protein and fat.</mark> <mark>This pattern is common in regions where grains are abundant but more expensive proteins and fats are inaccessible.</mark> <mark>The term "kwashiorkor" originates from a Ghanaian phrase meaning "the one who is deposed," referring to a child weaned from breast milk when a younger sibling is born, transitioning to a carbohydrate-rich, protein-poor diet.</mark>

<mark>In Western countries, kwashiorkor has been reported in infants fed exclusively on rice-based beverages ("rice milk") as substitutes for infant formula—often due to lower cost or perceived hypoallergenic benefits.</mark>

### <mark>Marasmic Kwashiorkor</mark>
<mark>A hybrid form of PEM, marasmic kwashiorkor, is characterized by both growth stunting and the presence of edema.</mark>

## Pathophysiology: Adapted vs. Nonadapted Starvation

The pathophysiology of PEM can be understood in terms of adapted and nonadapted starvation.

### <mark>Adapted Starvation (Marasmus)</mark>
<mark>In adapted starvation, chronic deficiency of all macronutrients—especially carbohydrates—leads to reduced insulin secretion.</mark> <mark>Catabolic hormones dominate, promoting glycogen breakdown into glucose.</mark> <mark>During the initial 24 hours, muscle protein is broken down to support gluconeogenesis.</mark> <mark>Subsequently, fat breakdown produces ketone bodies, which the brain and central nervous system can use, reducing the need for further muscle degradation and conserving lean body mass.</mark> <mark>However, in prolonged starvation, once fat and glycogen stores are depleted, lean tissue is consumed, ultimately leading to death if no nutrients are provided.</mark>

### <mark>Nonadapted Starvation (Kwashiorkor)</mark>
<mark>In nonadapted starvation, carbohydrate intake is relatively preserved while protein and fat intake are deficient.</mark> <mark>Insulin secretion continues due to carbohydrate availability, suppressing protein synthesis.</mark> <mark>This leads to:</mark>
- <mark>**Hypoproteinemia** and subsequent **edema**</mark>
- <mark>**Diarrhea**</mark>
- <mark>Impaired lipoprotein synthesis, resulting in **fatty liver**</mark>
- <mark>Failure to produce essential immune proteins, increasing susceptibility to **opportunistic infections** and **septicemia**, which are leading causes of death in kwashiorkor.</mark>

Despite the utility of the adapted vs. nonadapted starvation model, the precise reasons why some children develop marasmus while others develop kwashiorkor under similar conditions of starvation remain unclear and are a subject of ongoing debate.

## Clinical Findings

Childhood is a period of rapid growth and development, making it particularly vulnerable to nutritional deficits. Nutritional deprivation in this period often manifests as disruptions in normal growth patterns.

**Failure to thrive** is a hallmark of PEM and typically presents initially as **wasting**—poor weight gain or weight loss. Over time, it progresses to **stunting**, reflected in slowed linear growth.

## Management of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) in People Living with HIV

### Resistance to Anti-Herpes Drugs
Resistance to anti-herpes drugs is more common in individuals with HIV co-infection and is associated with treatment failure for genital herpes. Suppressive antiviral therapy with currently available agents has been shown in multiple studies to have no impact on HIV acquisition or transmission risk. Therefore, HSV treatment should not be used solely to manage or reduce HIV transmission or acquisition risk.

Much of the evidence on herpes management in people living with HIV comes from studies conducted before the widespread use of combination antiretroviral therapy (ART). <mark>Early prospective studies demonstrated that clinical lesions could be persistent and progressive in this population.</mark> Genital herpes, including chronic erosive lesions, may also occur as a manifestation of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) following the initiation of ART.

Patients with low CD4 counts are typically more susceptible to HSV-2 shedding, with a high risk of lesion development within the first 6 months after starting ART—particularly during the first 2 months. High levels of HSV viral shedding are associated with elevated HIV viral load prior to ART initiation. HSV-associated IRIS may be unresponsive to previously effective anti-herpes therapy, even in the absence of documented antiviral resistance. Management can be challenging; however, judicious use of prednisolone, as used in other forms of IRIS, may be beneficial.

---

### Management of Initial Episode HSV in People Living with HIV

<mark>There are no clinical trial data supporting the use of any antiviral for first-episode genital HSV specifically in people living with HIV.</mark> Most adults with HIV have serological evidence of prior HSV-1 and HSV-2 infection, making acquisition studies difficult to conduct.

Case reports suggest that primary genital HSV infection in this population may follow a prolonged and severe clinical course. Systemic symptoms may be prominent, and chronic lesions may develop if immunological clearance is impaired. In the absence of ART, primary genital herpes can be severe and prolonged, with progressive, multifocal, and coalescing mucocutaneous anogenital lesions. Serious complications—including meningitis, fulminant hepatitis, pneumonia, neurological disease, and disseminated infection—have been reported.

In the absence of definitive data, most experts recommend higher-than-standard antiviral dosing for initial HSV episodes in immunocompromised individuals. Some clinicians advocate a 10-day course at twice the standard dose of oral antivirals.

However, such intensified regimens may not be necessary for all people living with HIV, particularly those with normal CD4 counts.

For patients with advanced HIV disease:
- Double the standard dose of antiviral therapy should be considered.
- If new lesions continue to appear between Days 3 and 5 of treatment, the dose should be further increased.
- Early initiation of therapy is critical.
- If new lesions persist after 3–5 days, repeat viral isolation should be attempted, and susceptibility testing performed if possible.
- The antiviral dose should be escalated accordingly.

#### Recommended Initial Antiviral Doses for All People Living with HIV:
- **Aciclovir**: 400 mg five times daily for 7–10 days  
- **Valaciclovir**: 500 mg to 1 g twice daily for 10 days  
- **Famciclovir**: 250–500 mg three times daily for 10 days  

Treatment should last at least 10 days or until complete re-epithelialization of lesions—often longer than the standard duration used in HIV-negative individuals.

#### Management of Fulminant Disease:
If severe or disseminated disease occurs:
- Switch to intravenous aciclovir at 5–10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 2–7 days, or until clinical improvement.
- Follow with oral antiviral therapy to complete a minimum total of 10 days of treatment.

---

### Management of Recurrent HSV Disease in People Living with HIV

Both symptomatic and asymptomatic HSV reactivations are more frequent in people living with HIV. These recurrences may lead to persistent and progressive anogenital mucocutaneous lesions, especially when CD4 counts are below 50 cells/mm³. Lesions may be atypical, larger, deeper, and hypertrophic compared to those seen in immunocompetent individuals.

# <mark>Recurrent genital herpes</mark>

## <mark>Indications for therapy</mark>

Genital herpes recurrences are self-limiting and generally cause minor symptoms. The level of distress and the disruption to an individual's sexual and social life is often independent of the frequency of symptoms. Decisions about managing clinical recurrences should be made in partnership with the patient. Management strategies include supportive therapy only, episodic antiviral treatment, and suppressive antiviral therapy. The most appropriate strategy may vary over time depending on recurrence frequency, symptom severity, and relationship status. For most patients, supportive management is sufficient, with simple local measures such as saline baths or topical petroleum jelly being adequate.

## <mark>Episodic antiviral treatment</mark>

<mark>Oral aciclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir are effective in reducing the duration and severity of recurrent genital herpes, with a median reduction in healing time of 1–2 days.</mark> <mark>Head-to-head studies show no significant advantage of one agent over another, nor of extended 5-day regimens over ultra-short courses.</mark> <mark>Prodrugs (valaciclovir, famciclovir) offer simplified twice-daily dosing.</mark> <mark>Treatment initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset is most effective, with lesion abortion reported in up to one-third of patients when treatment is started early.</mark> <mark>To ensure prompt initiation, patients should keep a supply of medication available at all times and not wait to obtain it after symptoms begin.</mark>

### <mark>Initial short-course regimens:</mark>

- <mark>Aciclovir 800 mg three times daily for 2 days</mark>  
- <mark>Famciclovir 1 g twice daily for 1 day</mark>  
- <mark>Valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily for 3 days</mark>

### <mark>Alternative 5-day regimens:</mark>

- <mark>Aciclovir 400 mg three times daily</mark>  
- <mark>Aciclovir 200 mg five times daily</mark>  
- Valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily  
- <mark>Famciclovir 125 mg twice daily</mark>

## Suppressive therapy

Early trials of suppressive therapy focused on patients with ≥6 recurrences per year, but more recent studies include those with milder disease, showing benefit across all recurrence frequencies. The decision to initiate suppressive therapy is individualized, balancing recurrence frequency, personal impact, transmission concerns, and treatment burden.

Most patients experience a substantial reduction in recurrence frequency on suppressive antiviral therapy, although occasional symptomatic episodes may still occur.

Aciclovir has the most extensive long-term safety data (over 18 years of surveillance), with no evidence of cumulative toxicity or organ damage. Dose adjustment is required only in severe renal impairment. Routine blood monitoring is not recommended in otherwise healthy individuals. Periodic reassessment of the need for ongoing therapy is advisable, as patient circumstances may change. However, many patients do not experience significant changes in disease pattern after discontinuation, even following prolonged suppression.

A small number of immunocompetent patients continue to have frequent, virologically confirmed recurrences despite full-dose antiviral therapy. HSV resistance is unlikely in this group. Further immunological investigations are not useful beyond HIV testing. Interferon therapy is not recommended due to lack of robust evidence and limited availability.

## <mark>Recommended regimens</mark>

The optimal total daily dose for suppressive aciclovir therapy is 800 mg.

# <mark>INDICATIONS</mark>

- <mark>Treatment of initial and recurrent HSV genital infections</mark>  
- <mark>Suppression of frequently recurring genital HSV infections</mark>  
- Treatment of herpes zoster  

# DOSING REGIMENS

## INITIATION OF THERAPY

As with its parent compound, acyclovir, valacyclovir therapy should be initiated as soon as possible after the appearance of an HSV or VZV rash.

## <mark>RISKS AND PRECAUTIONS</mark>

<mark>In addition to the effects noted with acyclovir, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic uremic syndrome (TTP/HUS) has been observed in patients with advanced HIV disease and in transplant recipients receiving dosages of 8 g/day.</mark>

## <mark>COMPLICATIONS</mark>

Adverse effects are those that would be expected with acyclovir. <mark>However, severe and even fatal cases of TTP/HUS have been reported in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and transplant recipients taking high dosages of valacyclovir.</mark> <mark>The basis for these events and their causal relationship to valacyclovir have not been established.</mark> <mark>TTP/HUS has not been reported in patients taking conventional dosages (up to 3 g/day) of valacyclovir.</mark>

## TABLE 232-2: Dosing Regimens for Valacyclovir

| CONDITION | DOSAGE | ROUTE | DURATION |
|---------|--------|-------|----------|
| Primary HSV infection, immunocompetent host | 1000 mg bid | Oral | 10 days |
| Recurrent genital HSV infection, immunocompetent host | 500 mg bid | Oral | 3 days |
| Recurrent oral labial HSV infection, immunocompetent host | 2000 mg bid | Oral | 1 day |
| Oral labial HSV infection, immunocompromised host | 500 mg bid | Oral | 5–10 days |
| Chronic suppression of HSV infection | 1000 mg qd | Oral | Undefined/indefinite |
| Varicella: adolescent/adult | 1000 mg tid | Oral | 5 days |
| Herpes zoster: normal host or not severe disease in immunocompromised host | 1000 mg tid | Oral | 7 days |

HSV = herpes simplex virus.

# Famciclovir and Penciclovir

## MECHANISM OF ACTION

Famciclovir (9-[4-hydroxy-3-hydroxymethylbut-1-yl] guanine) is a prodrug of penciclovir (9-[4-hydroxy-3-hydroxymethylbut-1-yl] guanine). Penciclovir is phosphorylated to penciclovir triphosphate. The initial phosphorylation of penciclovir to penciclovir monophosphate is mediated by HSV- or VZV-induced thymidine kinases, similar to the activation of acyclovir. Subsequent phosphorylation to the diphosphate and triphosphate forms is carried out by cellular kinases. Penciclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerases and interferes with extension of the nascent viral DNA chain. Due to the presence of a hydroxyl group on the acyclic side chain of penciclovir, limited DNA chain extension may still occur.

## PHARMACOKINETICS

Famciclovir is available as an oral formulation and is converted to penciclovir by deacetylation and oxidation in the liver and intestine. The bioavailability of famciclovir is 77%. After oral administration of 500 mg famciclovir, a peak plasma concentration of penciclovir (3.3 μg/mL) is reached within 1 hour.

## HSV Suppression in People Living with HIV

<mark>For **valaciclovir**, multiple studies have evaluated its role in suppressing recurrent genital herpes.</mark> <mark>High-dose regimens (2 g four times daily) have been investigated in immunocompromised populations, including those with HIV and individuals recovering from bone marrow transplants.</mark> <mark>More recently, numerous trials have assessed the efficacy of **aciclovir** and **valaciclovir** for HSV suppression and their impact on HIV transmission in co-infected individuals.</mark> <mark>These studies show that oral **aciclovir** at standard doses, as well as **valaciclovir** at 1 g once daily or 500 mg twice daily, are associated with minimal to no adverse effects or toxicity compared to HIV-negative individuals.</mark> However, **high-dose valaciclovir (8 g daily)** has been linked to **microangiopathic haemolytic uraemic syndrome**.

### Recommended Regimens for Daily HSV Suppressive Therapy in HIV-Positive Individuals:
- <mark>**Aciclovir 400 mg** orally twice to three times a day</mark>  
- <mark>**Valaciclovir 500 mg** orally twice a day</mark>  

<mark>If these regimens fail to control outbreaks, the first step is to **double the dose**.</mark> If suppression remains inadequate, **famciclovir 500 mg** orally twice a day may be considered (evidence level: 1, B).

---

## HSV Suppression and HIV Progression

<mark>Suppressive antiviral therapy with **aciclovir** or **valaciclovir** has been shown to reduce HIV viraemia in patients with detectable viral loads, although the exact mechanism remains unclear.</mark> <mark>This effect can influence HIV disease progression, particularly in individuals **not on antiretroviral therapy (ART)**.</mark>

A large randomized controlled trial (RCT) in patients with early HIV (not on ART, CD4 counts >250 cells/mm³) demonstrated that **aciclovir 400 mg twice daily** helped maintain CD4 counts above 250 cells/mm³, reducing the need for initiating ART by **16%** at 2 years in the treatment group.

However, **no significant benefit** of HSV suppressive therapy has been observed in individuals already receiving effective ART. Since effective ART remains the cornerstone of HIV management—both for individual health and prevention of transmission—**HSV suppression for the purpose of controlling HIV progression is not considered clinically relevant** in the modern treatment era.

---

## Management of Recalcitrant Herpes in Immunocompromised Individuals

Clinically refractory genital herpes, while rare in immunocompetent individuals, is a significant issue in those with severe immunodeficiency, such as in late-stage HIV.

### Treatment Approach:
- <mark>**Systemic therapy with foscarnet or cidofovir** is preferred for drug-resistant HSV in HIV-positive patients.</mark>
- Evidence supports **alternating aciclovir and cidofovir** for recurrent episodes, which may help reduce the emergence of cidofovir-resistant strains.
- However, the **efficacy, safety, and durability** of these treatments require further evaluation in prospective, controlled trials.

### Aciclovir Resistance:
- Aciclovir-resistant HSV strains are found in approximately **5–7%** of genital herpes isolates from people with HIV.
- Resistance is confirmed when isolates require **aciclovir concentrations >1–3 mg/L** for inhibition.
- Most commonly, resistance arises from mutations in the **HSV thymidine kinase (TK) gene**, which impairs the initial phosphorylation of aciclovir.
  - Mutations may lead to TK with reduced affinity for aciclovir or complete absence of TK production.
- **TK-deficient strains** are less pathogenic in immunocompetent hosts but can cause severe local or disseminated disease in immunocompromised individuals.
- These strains appear less capable of establishing latency; thus, subsequent recurrences are often due to **aciclovir-sensitive isolates**.

### Treatment Implications:
- **Partially resistant strains** may respond to high-dose intravenous aciclovir or other nucleoside analogues.
- **Fully resistant strains** are cross-resistant to **valaciclovir** and **ganciclovir**, and most are also resistant to **famciclovir**.

## <mark>Immune Surveillance and Skin Cancer Risk</mark>

<mark>Several lines of evidence challenge the interpretation of immune surveillance as the primary mechanism protecting against skin cancer.</mark> Cyclophosphamide is a well-known mutagen, and cyclosporine promotes tumor growth in vitro and in immune-deficient mice—organisms that lack an immune system to suppress—suggesting direct carcinogenic effects independent of immunosuppression. <mark>Azathioprine acts as a mutagen when combined with UVA irradiation.</mark> While HIV patients have a modestly increased incidence of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), these tumors often occur at sun-shielded sites and are associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.

Skin cancers are frequently reported in patients with leukemia or lymphoma, conditions that involve immunodeficiency. <mark>Although many published studies lack controls or detailed patient data, an approximately eightfold increased risk of skin cancer in chronic lymphocytic leukemia appears valid.</mark> However, most of these patients have also been exposed to immunosuppressive drugs or radiation, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of immune suppression from the mutagenic effects of prior treatments.

<mark>In contrast, Merkel cell carcinoma appears to be genuinely sensitive to immune function.</mark> Its incidence increases 10- to 20-fold in solid-organ transplant recipients and approximately 13-fold in HIV patients and those with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (see Chap. 120). The risk of metastasis and mortality is also elevated across all types of immunosuppressed patients. Regardless of the underlying mechanism, close monitoring of immunosuppressed individuals is essential, as early detection allows for curative treatment even in this high-risk population.

---

## Animal Models of Skin Cancer: Clinical Implications

### <mark>Genetic Risk Factors for Ultraviolet Radiation Carcinogenesis</mark>

#### <mark>Pigmentation and Initial Damage</mark>

<mark>Melanin plays a critical role in protecting the skin against cancer development.</mark> <mark>The Fitzpatrick skin phototype classification (see Chap.</mark> <mark>89), which considers both baseline pigmentation and response to ultraviolet radiation (UVR)—such as tendency to burn or tan—can account for up to a 100-fold difference in skin cancer susceptibility.</mark>

<mark>Individuals with oculocutaneous albinism, characterized by deficient melanin production due to various genetic mutations, face a markedly increased risk of skin cancer (see Chap.</mark> 71). <mark>This risk primarily involves non-melanoma skin cancers, though melanoma incidence is also elevated.</mark>

<mark>Another hereditary risk factor—red or blonde hair—is linked to polymorphisms in the **melanocortin 1 receptor** (MC1R) (see Chap.</mark> 70). <mark>This G-protein coupled receptor binds melanocyte-stimulating hormone and is central to melanogenesis.</mark> <mark>Certain loss-of-function mutations result in the production of **pheomelanin** instead of the more photoprotective **eumelanin**.</mark>

<mark>This distinction is crucial for skin cancer prevention.</mark> <mark>Pheomelanin is a poor free radical scavenger; upon UVR exposure, it degrades and generates superoxide radicals.</mark> <mark>Thus, pheomelanin can act as a photosensitizer, contributing to oxidative stress and even inducing apoptosis in neighboring cells.</mark> <mark>The combination of reduced protection and increased oxidative damage in the epidermis likely contributes to the heightened skin cancer risk observed in red-haired individuals.</mark>

<mark>Reactive oxygen species are normally neutralized by antioxidants such as glutathione.</mark> <mark>Polymorphisms in genes encoding **glutathione S-transferase** are associated with a twofold increased risk of actinic keratosis (AK), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and basal cell carcinoma (BCC).</mark> <mark>This risk escalates to sixfold in individuals with high sun exposure and reaches 12-fold in sun-exposed transplant recipients.</mark>

#### DNA Repair and Apoptosis

Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) (see Chap. 109) exemplifies the link between DNA repair capacity and skin cancer risk. Mutations in any of the XP genes impair nucleotide excision repair (NER), and the clinical severity—measured by tumor burden and life expectancy—correlates directly with residual DNA repair function.

This relationship extends to the general population. Patients with actinic keratosis exhibit 30% to 50% reduced excision repair capacity in normal fibroblasts or lymphocytes. Similarly, cells from individuals with basal cell carcinoma (BCC) show diminished excision repair compared to those from healthy controls. These findings indicate that even subtle variations in DNA repair efficiency can significantly influence an individual’s susceptibility to skin cancer.

## <mark>ULTRAVIOLET RADIATION CARCINOGENESIS</mark>

### <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

- Ultraviolet radiation (UVR) from the sun is the most prevalent carcinogen in humans, particularly among Caucasians.  
- <mark>Annual increases continue in the incidence of all types of skin cancer.</mark>  
- The importance of exposure timing, dose rate, and total UVR exposure differ between the types of skin cancer.  
- Sunlight leaves characteristic mutations that identify key molecular and cellular steps in skin tumor development.  
- DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell signaling pathways are critical to preventing skin cancer, and UVR affects each of these processes.  
- <mark>Genetic polymorphisms in genes for DNA repair, melanin, and free radical scavenging affect skin cancer risk.</mark>  
- Novel, pathway-based approaches to prevent or treat skin cancer are being developed.  
- Educational and behavioral approaches are key to minimizing skin cancer rates in the future.

---

A non-CSD (chronic sun-damaged) route involves intermittent sun exposure of sites such as the trunk. <mark>Non-CSD melanomas carry mutations in the **BRAF** or **NRAS** oncogenes—upstream regulators of cell cycle genes—and the patients often have variant alleles of the **melanocortin 1 receptor**.</mark> Intermittently exposed body sites are the locations of the rising melanoma incidence in recent decades, melanomas in patients younger than age 50 years, and increased melanoma rates near the equator. Recreational sunburn may explain these trends and the twofold higher melanoma incidence in office workers compared to outdoor workers.

<mark>Sunlight is also implicated by the susceptible population: both melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers are more frequent in light-skinned individuals with blonde or red hair who burn rather than tan.</mark> Compared to black-skinned individuals, non-melanoma skin cancer risk increases approximately 10-fold in Asians and 100-fold in Caucasians, with an additional 2- to 12-fold increased risk associated with blonde or, especially, red hair. The disparity is less pronounced for melanoma, with a risk ratio of approximately 1:1:15. In black skin, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is rare even in patients with hereditary nevoid BCC syndrome (NBCCS or Gorlin syndrome). Skin tumors in black patients are often scar-related, though these may also be associated with sunlight.

<mark>Melanin-related effects contribute to skin cancer risk through several mechanisms: reduced total melanin in light skin, less protective capacity of pheomelanin compared to eumelanin, and greater production of photosensitized reactive oxygen species by pheomelanin.</mark>

Molecular epidemiology provides the most direct evidence for ultraviolet radiation (UVR) as the carcinogenic component of sunlight: **UVB signature mutations** are found in human BCC, SCC, and actinic keratosis (AK). Mutant cells are typically located in areas with elastotic dermis, indicating chronic sun exposure.

UVB is particularly effective as a carcinogen because it partially penetrates the ozone layer and the stratum corneum and is readily absorbed by DNA. The ozone layer absorbs all but 1 part per million of UVC (which is lethal and used in germicidal lamps), while UVA penetrates deeply but is poorly absorbed by DNA. Nevertheless, chronic UVA exposure can induce tumors in mice and can malignantly transform predisposed human cells.

The cumulative sunlight exposure required to cause BCC or SCC in adults is substantial—approximately 10,000 hours for BCC and 70,000 hours for SCC. Psoriasis patients receiving fewer than 100 UVB treatments (with low psoralen plus UVA [PUVA] exposure) had a slightly elevated risk of SCC or BCC on sun-shielded sites, while those receiving more than 300 UVB treatments had a threefold higher risk.

# <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

<mark>Rubella is an enveloped RNA virus in the Togaviridae family.</mark> <mark>The virus is spread through direct or droplet contact from nasopharyngeal secretions.</mark> Infected individuals shed virus for 5 to 7 days before and up to 14 days after the onset of disease, with viremia unlikely after the rash appears. <mark>In most individuals, infection leads to lifelong immunity.</mark>

Congenital rubella occurs when a nonimmunized, susceptible pregnant woman is exposed to the virus. Transplacental infection of the fetus occurs during the viremic stage. The risk is greatest when fetal exposure happens in the first trimester. Congenitally infected infants may shed the virus through urine, blood, and nasopharyngeal secretions for up to 12 months after birth, making them a potential source of infection for other susceptible individuals.

# <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

## <mark>History</mark>

Primary rubella infection is typically a mild, subclinical disease, particularly in adults. <mark>The prodrome includes low-grade fever, myalgias, headache, conjunctivitis, rhinitis, cough, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.</mark> <mark>These symptoms may last up to 4 days and often resolve as the rash appears.</mark> <mark>Up to 50% of children with primary rubella infection may have a subclinical course or present with lymphadenopathy or rash alone (without prodrome).</mark> <mark>In contrast, older adults may experience more severe and prolonged prodromal symptoms, which can make clinical differentiation from rubeola (measles) difficult.</mark> <mark>The presence of Koplik spots in the oral mucosa favors rubeola.</mark>

<mark>As the prodrome resolves and the rash develops, some patients may exhibit an enanthem consisting of tiny red macules on the soft palate and uvula (Forschheimer spots).</mark> <mark>This finding is not diagnostic for rubella.</mark>

## <mark>Cutaneous Lesions</mark>

<mark>The exanthem appears 14 to 17 days after exposure and consists of pruritic pink to red macules and papules that begin on the face and rapidly spread to the neck, trunk, and extremities.</mark> <mark>Lesions on the trunk may coalesce, while those on the extremities tend to remain discrete.</mark> <mark>The rash typically lasts 2 to 3 days, in contrast to rubeola, which persists longer and clears starting from the head and neck.</mark> <mark>Desquamation may occur after the rash resolves.</mark>

## <mark>Related Physical Findings</mark>

<mark>Lymphadenopathy is most prominent in the posterior cervical, suboccipital, and postauricular lymph nodes and may be noted up to 7 days before rash onset.</mark> <mark>Node enlargement can persist for several weeks.</mark>

Arthritis occurs in up to 70% of infected adults, particularly women. Both small and large joints may be involved. Joint symptoms often begin as the rash fades and can last for several weeks. In some cases, symptoms may become persistent or recurrent, and joint swelling may progress to effusion.

# Laboratory Tests

A complete blood cell count typically shows leukopenia with relative neutropenia.
